sections.title: Indian Society in the 19th and 20th Centuries

blocks.text: Colonial rule produced major changes in rural society, education, communication, social institutions and economic relations. These changes were uneven and interacted with older social structures.

Major changes under colonial rule included new land revenue systems and property rights, commercialisation of agriculture, deindustrialisation of handicrafts, the growth of port cities (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras), railways (from 1853), the telegraph and the postal system, English education, the printing press and the rise of a Western-educated middle class. Census operations (from 1871-1872) classified people by caste and religion, which some historians (Nicholas Dirks) argue made caste identities more rigid.

At the same time, older structures - caste, joint family, religious authority, village hierarchies - continued and adapted. Social reform and religious revival movements, caste associations and anti-caste movements (Jyotirao Phule's Satyashodhak Samaj, 1873; the Self-Respect Movement of E. V. Ramasamy 'Periyar', 1925; Ambedkar's campaigns) emerged as responses. Change was uneven: cities and educated groups changed faster than villages, and benefits went mainly to upper castes and classes.
Colonial land revenue arrangements attempted to secure regular state income from agriculture. They changed relations among the colonial state, landlords, intermediaries and cultivators.

Permanent Settlement (1793, Cornwallis): in Bengal, Bihar and Odisha, zamindars became proprietors with revenue fixed in perpetuity; the Sunset Law auctioned estates for non-payment; it created a loyal landlord class but left peasants unprotected (until Tenancy Acts of 1859 and 1885). Ryotwari (Munro and Read, from 1820, Madras and Bombay): direct settlement with cultivators; revenue was high (up to half the net produce) and revised periodically. Mahalwari (1822 Holt Mackenzie; 1833 revised under Bentinck by R. M. Bird and James Thomason; North-Western Provinces, Punjab, Central India): revenue fixed for the village or estate (mahal), collected through the headman or lambardar.

Together they covered about 19 percent (Permanent), 51 percent (Ryotwari) and 30 percent (Mahalwari) of British India's area. Common effects: land became a marketable commodity; high cash demands forced peasants to borrow; land passed to moneylenders and merchants; absentee landlordism and subinfeudation grew; and agricultural investment remained low.
Commercialisation meant the growing production of crops for sale in markets rather than mainly for local consumption. It connected peasants more closely with prices, traders and credit.

From the mid-nineteenth century, peasants increasingly grew cash crops - cotton (especially during the American Civil War, 1861-1865, when British mills needed Indian cotton), jute, indigo, opium, tea, sugarcane, groundnut and wheat for export. Railways and the Suez Canal (1869) connected the interior to ports and world markets.

Some richer peasants benefited, but for most, commercialisation was 'forced' by the need to pay revenue in cash and debts. Peasants became vulnerable to world price fluctuations (the cotton boom and crash of the 1860s led to the Deccan Riots of 1875; the Great Depression of 1929-1933 ruined many). Food crop areas declined in some regions, increasing the impact of famines. Indigo planters forced Bengali peasants to grow indigo, leading to the Indigo Revolt (1859-1860), dramatised in Dinabandhu Mitra's 'Nil Darpan'.
Rural society included cultivators with different levels of land control as well as landless labourers. Colonial economic pressures often increased insecurity among poorer rural groups.

Rural society was stratified: landlords (zamindars, taluqdars), rich peasants (often called jotedars in Bengal), middle peasants who owned and cultivated their land, poor peasants, tenants-at-will, sharecroppers (bargadars, adhiars) and landless agricultural labourers, many of them Dalits. Bonded labour (such as the kamia and hali systems) existed in many regions.

The number of landless labourers increased under colonial rule - from about 7.5 million in 1882 to over 30 million by 1931 according to census estimates - due to loss of land to moneylenders, deindustrialisation pushing artisans into agriculture, population growth and fragmentation of holdings. Peasant movements included the Deccan Riots (1875), Pabna agrarian leagues (1873-1876), the Moplah uprisings, the Champaran and Kheda satyagrahas (1917-1918), the Bardoli satyagraha (1928) and the Tebhaga (1946) and Telangana (1946-1951) movements.
Many peasants depended on loans for cultivation, revenue payments and consumption. High debt could increase dependence on moneylenders and deepen rural distress.

Moneylenders (sahukars, mahajans, banias, Chettiars, Pathans and Marwaris) supplied credit at high interest - often 24 to 60 percent a year or more. Peasants borrowed to pay land revenue, buy seed and cattle, survive bad seasons, and for marriages and ceremonies. Under colonial law, land could be mortgaged and sold through civil courts, so debt led to loss of land. The Deccan Riots Commission (1878) and the Famine Commission reports documented the problem.

Government measures included the Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act (1879), the Punjab Land Alienation Act (1900, restricting transfer of land from agricultural to non-agricultural castes), the Cooperative Credit Societies Act (1904) and the Cooperative Societies Act (1912), and debt relief legislation by Congress ministries in 1937-1939. The Royal Commission on Agriculture (1928) and the Central Banking Enquiry Committee (1931) estimated rural debt in the hundreds of crores of rupees.

sections.title: Trading Economy: Surat, Bengal and Coromandel

blocks.text: These regions were important centres of Indian and overseas trade. The eighteenth century brought changes in commercial routes, merchant networks and the balance of economic power.

Surat was the main port of the Mughal empire in the seventeenth century, with merchants such as Virji Vora and Mulla Abdul Ghafur trading to the Red Sea and Persian Gulf. Its decline in the eighteenth century resulted from the decline of the Mughals and the Safavids, Maratha raids (Shivaji sacked Surat in 1664 and 1670), the rise of Bombay under English control and the English taking over the castle of Surat (1759).

Bengal was the richest province, exporting cotton textiles (muslin of Dhaka), silk, saltpetre, sugar and rice; European companies bought heavily with silver. After Plassey (1757), the Company and its servants used political power to control trade and weavers, and the 'investment' was financed from Bengal revenue rather than imported silver. The Coromandel coast (Masulipatnam, Pulicat, Madras) exported textiles to Southeast Asia and Europe; it was affected by wars and the shift of trade to English hands. Historians such as Ashin Das Gupta, Om Prakash and P. J. Marshall studied these changes.
India had established indigenous systems of credit and finance. Colonial rule also encouraged new forms of modern banking linked to expanding trade and industry.

Indigenous banking included shroffs (sarrafs), mahajans and great banking families such as the Jagat Seths of Murshidabad, who acted as bankers to the Nawabs of Bengal and the Company; the Nattukottai Chettiars of Tamil Nadu, who financed trade in Burma, Ceylon and Southeast Asia; and the Marwaris and Multanis. They used hundis (bills of exchange) to transfer money across long distances, accepted deposits and lent to merchants, peasants and rulers.

Modern banking began with agency houses in Calcutta. The Bank of Hindostan (1770), the Bank of Bengal (1806), Bank of Bombay (1840) and Bank of Madras (1843) were founded; these three presidency banks merged into the Imperial Bank of India (1921), which became the State Bank of India (1955). The first bank with Indian management was the Oudh Commercial Bank (1881); the Punjab National Bank (1894) was founded by Lala Lajpat Rai and others. The Swadeshi movement encouraged Indian banks. The Reserve Bank of India was established in 1935.
Cotton, tea, jute and steel became important modern industries. Their growth introduced factory production but occurred within the wider structure of the colonial economy.

Cotton: the first successful cotton mill was founded by Cowasji Nanabhoy Davar in Bombay (1854); by 1914 there were over 270 mills, mainly in Bombay and Ahmedabad, owned by Indians (Parsis, Gujaratis, Marwaris). Jute: the first mill was set up at Rishra near Calcutta (1855) by George Acland; jute mills along the Hooghly were dominated by British and Scottish capital. Tea: plantations in Assam began in the 1830s-1840s (the Assam Company, 1839), using indentured 'coolie' labour recruited from central and eastern India under harsh conditions.

Steel: Jamsetji Tata planned an iron and steel industry; the Tata Iron and Steel Company was founded in 1907 at Sakchi (Jamshedpur) and began production in 1912; the Indian Iron and Steel Company (Burnpur, 1918) followed. Industrial growth was limited by colonial policies (free trade, lack of tariff protection until 1920s, railway freight policies that favoured imports and exports), British managing agencies and lack of capital goods industries. Factory workers faced long hours and low wages, leading to Factory Acts (1881, 1891, 1911) and trade unions.

sections.title: Reforms under Cornwallis, Bentinck and Dalhousie

blocks.text: The syllabus groups these administrators under modernisation and reform. Their policies affected administration, law, education, communication and colonial governance.

Cornwallis (1786-1793): the Permanent Settlement; civil service reforms (higher salaries, ban on private trade, exclusion of Indians from higher posts); judicial reforms (district courts, the Cornwallis Code of 1793, separating revenue and judicial functions); and police reforms (thanas under darogas). Bentinck (1828-1835): abolition of sati (Regulation XVII, 1829), suppression of thuggee (with William Sleeman), measures against female infanticide, Macaulay's Minute on Education and the English Education Act (1835), making English the language of higher education and administration, appointment of Indians as deputy collectors and judges, and the Charter Act of 1833.

Dalhousie (1848-1856): railways (Bombay to Thane, 16 April 1853), the electric telegraph (1853-1854), the postal reform with uniform postage stamps (1854), the Public Works Department, the Ganges Canal (1854), Wood's Despatch on Education (1854), the Widow Remarriage Act (passed 1856) and an aggressive annexation policy. These 'modernising' reforms strengthened colonial control while also introducing new institutions and ideas.
Western-style modern education expanded under colonial rule. It helped produce an educated middle class and new forms of intellectual and political debate.

Early efforts included Warren Hastings' Calcutta Madrasa (1781), Jonathan Duncan's Sanskrit College at Benares (1791), Fort William College (1800), and missionary schools at Serampore. The Charter Act of 1813 provided one lakh rupees for education. The Orientalist-Anglicist controversy was settled by Macaulay's Minute (1835), which favoured English and Western learning, intending to create 'a class of persons Indian in blood and colour, but English in tastes, in opinions, in morals and in intellect' (the 'downward filtration' theory).

Wood's Despatch (1854), the 'Magna Carta of English education in India', recommended a system from primary schools to universities, grants-in-aid, teacher training and women's education. Universities were established at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras (1857). The Hunter Commission (1882) emphasised primary education; Curzon's Indian Universities Act (1904) increased government control; the Sadler Commission (1917) and Wardha scheme of basic education (Gandhi, 1937) followed. Modern education created a middle class that led reform and nationalism, but literacy remained low (about 12 percent in 1947).
Newspapers and journals became important for social reform, public debate and later nationalist political consciousness.

James Augustus Hicky's 'Bengal Gazette' (1780) was the first newspaper in India. Indian-run papers followed: Rammohun Roy's 'Sambad Kaumudi' (Bengali, 1821) and 'Mirat-ul-Akbar' (Persian, 1822); 'The Hindu' (1878); Tilak's 'Kesari' (Marathi) and 'Mahratta' (English) (1881); Surendranath Banerjea's 'The Bengalee'; the 'Amrita Bazar Patrika' (1868); and Gandhi's 'Young India' and 'Harijan'. The vernacular press spread news and ideas widely, even to the illiterate through public reading.

The government tried to control the press: Lord Wellesley's Censorship Act (1799), Adam's regulations (1823), Charles Metcalfe's liberation of the press (1835), Lord Lytton's Vernacular Press Act (1878, the 'gagging act', repealed by Ripon in 1882), the Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act (1908), the Indian Press Act (1910) and wartime censorship. Tilak was imprisoned for his writings (1897 and 1908). The press became a key instrument of social reform and nationalism.
An educated intelligentsia emerged through modern education and print culture. It played an important role in reform, criticism of social practices and political discussion.

The modern intelligentsia emerged from English education and print culture, mainly in the presidency towns. Important early members included Rammohun Roy, the 'Young Bengal' group of Henry Derozio at Hindu College (who questioned tradition radically in the 1820s-1830s), Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, Dadabhai Naoroji, M. G. Ranade, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Syed Ahmad Khan, Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay and Rabindranath Tagore.

The intelligentsia wrote, debated and formed associations - the Landholders' Society (1838), British Indian Association (1851), Bombay Association (1852), Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870), Indian Association (1876) and Madras Mahajan Sabha (1884) - that led to the Congress (1885). The period is often called the 'Bengal Renaissance' or 'Indian Renaissance', although historians note that the intelligentsia was drawn mostly from upper castes and that its ideas reached limited sections of society.
Debates over women's education, social status and oppressive customs became an important part of nineteenth- and twentieth-century reform.

Reforms targeted sati (abolished 1829), female infanticide (laws of 1795, 1804 and 1870), child marriage (the Age of Consent Act 1891; the Sarda Act 1929 fixing the minimum age at 14 for girls and 18 for boys), widow remarriage (1856 Act), polygamy and purdah, and the denial of education. Women's education grew through Bethune School (Calcutta, 1849), the Phules' schools in Pune (from 1848), missionary schools and later women's colleges such as SNDT Women's University (D. K. Karve, 1916).

Women reformers and writers included Pandita Ramabai, Tarabai Shinde, Savitribai Phule, Sarojini Naidu, Begum Rokeya and Ramabai Ranade. Women's organisations (WIA 1917, AIWC 1927) and participation in the freedom struggle increased their public role. The Constitution (1950) and the Hindu Code Bills (1955-1956) gave legal equality. Historians observe that early reforms aimed partly at creating educated wives and mothers rather than full equality.
The Brahmo Samaj was a major socio-religious reform movement associated with criticism of certain social and religious practices and the promotion of reform.

Raja Rammohun Roy (1772-1833) founded the Atmiya Sabha (1815) and the Brahmo Sabha (1828), later called the Brahmo Samaj. He advocated monotheism based on the Upanishads, opposed idol worship, polytheism, caste rigidity and superstition, campaigned against sati, supported women's property rights and Western education (he supported the founding of Hindu College, 1817). He is called the 'father of the Indian Renaissance'. He died in Bristol, England, in 1833.

Debendranath Tagore revived the Samaj (Tattvabodhini Sabha, 1839). Keshab Chandra Sen made it more radical, supporting inter-caste marriage and women's emancipation; the Native Marriage Act (Brahmo Marriage Act, 1872) followed. Splits occurred: the Adi Brahmo Samaj (Debendranath) and the Brahmo Samaj of India (Keshab, 1866), and later the Sadharan Brahmo Samaj (1878) after Keshab married his under-age daughter to the prince of Cooch Behar. The Samaj influenced Bengali culture and spread reform ideas, though its membership was small.
The Arya Samaj was a reform movement that sought religious and social renewal through a return to Vedic authority.

Swami Dayanand Saraswati (1824-1883) founded the Arya Samaj in Bombay in 1875; its headquarters moved to Lahore. His book 'Satyarth Prakash' (1875) argued that the Vedas were the source of all truth, and he gave the slogan 'Back to the Vedas'. He rejected idol worship, polytheism, the Puranas, rituals, priestly domination, untouchability, caste by birth, child marriage and the ban on widow remarriage, and supported women's education and the use of Hindi.

The Samaj started the shuddhi movement to reconvert those who had converted to Islam or Christianity, which contributed to communal tensions. After Dayanand's death, it split into the 'College' group (Lala Hansraj, Lala Lajpat Rai), which founded the Dayanand Anglo-Vedic (DAV) schools and colleges (DAV College Lahore, 1886), and the 'Gurukul' group (Swami Shraddhanand), which founded the Gurukul Kangri at Haridwar (1902) based on traditional education. The Arya Samaj was strong in Punjab and western Uttar Pradesh and influenced nationalism there.
The Ramakrishna Mission combined spiritual ideas with organised social and educational service.

Ramakrishna Paramahamsa (1836-1886), a priest at the Dakshineswar temple near Calcutta, practised various spiritual paths - Hindu, Muslim and Christian - and taught that all religions lead to the same God ('as many faiths, so many paths'). His disciple Narendranath Datta, Swami Vivekananda (1863-1902), founded the Ramakrishna Mission at Belur in 1897 to carry out social service: schools, hospitals, orphanages and famine relief.

Vivekananda's speech at the Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago (1893), beginning 'Sisters and brothers of America', made Hinduism (Vedanta) known in the West. He emphasised practical Vedanta, service to humanity as worship of God ('daridra narayana'), self-confidence, strength ('Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached') and criticised caste rigidity and superstition. He inspired nationalist youth; his birthday (12 January) is National Youth Day.
The Aligarh Movement promoted modern education among Indian Muslims and became associated particularly with Sir Syed Ahmad Khan.

Sir Syed Ahmad Khan (1817-1898), a judicial officer in the Company's service who remained loyal in 1857, believed that Muslims had fallen behind after the decline of Mughal rule and the revolt because they rejected Western education. He wrote 'The Causes of the Indian Revolt' (1859), founded the Scientific Society (1864) to translate Western works into Urdu, started the journal 'Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq', and founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental (MAO) College at Aligarh (1875), which became Aligarh Muslim University in 1920.

He interpreted the Quran rationally, arguing that it did not conflict with modern science, opposed purdah and polygamy, and supported women's education. Politically, he advised Muslims to stay away from the Congress and to cooperate with the British, fearing Hindu majority domination in representative institutions. The Aligarh Movement created a modern Muslim educated class (associates included Chiragh Ali, Altaf Hussain Hali, Nazir Ahmad and Shibli Nomani) and influenced later Muslim politics, including the Muslim League.
Reform movements encouraged debate on religion, education, caste, women and social change, while their reach and outlook varied.

Positive impacts: the movements criticised superstition, idolatry, caste rigidity, untouchability and the oppression of women; encouraged education (including women's education) and rational thought; created new institutions (schools, colleges, newspapers, welfare organisations); promoted pride in Indian culture and self-confidence against colonial claims of superiority; and prepared the ground for nationalism.

Limitations: they were led mainly by the urban, upper-caste and educated middle class, so they reached few peasants and lower castes; some depended on colonial legislation; some revivalist movements emphasised a glorious Hindu or Islamic past, contributing to communal consciousness (shuddhi and tabligh campaigns). Lower-caste movements (Phule's Satyashodhak Samaj, Sree Narayana Guru's movement in Kerala - 'one caste, one religion, one God for man' -, Periyar's Self-Respect Movement, Ambedkar's campaigns) challenged the caste system more fundamentally.

sections.title: Rural Economy and Society under Colonial Rule

blocks.text:
Rural India remained central to the colonial economy. Land revenue settlements linked agriculture closely to colonial fiscal needs and altered relations among the state, landlords and cultivators.

Commercialisation of agriculture encouraged production for markets, but market dependence also exposed cultivators to price changes and debt. Peasants and landless labourers did not experience these developments equally.

Rural credit became crucial, and indebtedness was a serious problem for many cultivators. Colonial rural society therefore combined economic change with persistent inequality and insecurity.

Land revenue systems: the Permanent Settlement created zamindars as proprietors but left peasants at their mercy, the Ryotwari system made cultivators pay high, periodically revised revenue directly to the state, and the Mahalwari system made villages jointly responsible. All demanded revenue in cash and enforced it strictly; land became saleable, creating a land market, and heavy demands often exceeded what peasants could pay. In Bengal, the Rent Acts of 1859 and the Bengal Tenancy Act (1885) gave some protection to tenants.

Commercialisation: railways, the Suez Canal and colonial demand led to cash crops (cotton, jute, indigo, opium, tea, wheat). It benefited some rich peasants, merchants and moneylenders, but most peasants were 'forced' into commercial agriculture to pay revenue and debts and were exposed to price fluctuations; food security declined, contributing to famines (1876-1878, 1896-1897, 1899-1900, Bengal 1943, which killed about 3 million). Social differentiation: the growth of tenancy, sharecropping and landless labour, partly due to the decline of handicrafts.

Credit and indebtedness: moneylenders charged high interest and acquired peasants' land through courts. Responses included peasant revolts (Indigo 1859-1860, Pabna 1873-1876, Deccan Riots 1875) and colonial laws (Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act 1879, Punjab Land Alienation Act 1900, cooperative credit societies 1904). Historians debate whether colonial agriculture stagnated (most nationalist and Marxist historians) or grew in some regions (Punjab canal colonies). The overall picture is one of change combined with poverty and insecurity.

The eighteenth-century trading economy included important centres such as Surat, Bengal and the Coromandel coast. Political and commercial changes altered older routes and merchant networks.

Indigenous bankers and credit institutions continued to operate, while modern banking developed under colonial conditions. Modern industries such as cotton, tea, jute and steel expanded during the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

Industrialisation created new factories and workers but did not remove the colonial character of the economy.

Trading economy in the eighteenth century: Surat declined with the Mughals and the rise of Bombay; Bengal's export trade in textiles, silk and saltpetre came under Company control after Plassey, with weavers forced to sell to the Company at low prices; the Coromandel textile trade shifted to English control. The 'drain' began as Bengal revenue financed Company exports. Indian merchants and bankers (Jagat Seths, Chettiars, Marwaris) adapted - some collaborated with the Company, while others were marginalised.

Banking: indigenous bankers with hundis continued to dominate internal trade finance. Modern banking began with agency houses and presidency banks (Bank of Bengal 1806, Bombay 1840, Madras 1843), merged into the Imperial Bank (1921); Indian joint-stock banks (Oudh Commercial Bank 1881, Punjab National Bank 1894, Bank of India 1906) grew, especially during the Swadeshi movement; the Reserve Bank of India was founded in 1935.

Industry: modern industries emerged - cotton textiles (Bombay 1854, Ahmedabad), jute (Calcutta 1855), tea plantations (Assam), coal (Raniganj), railways workshops, and iron and steel (TISCO 1907). However, deindustrialisation of handicrafts, British control of jute, tea and mining through managing agencies, lack of capital goods and tariff protection limited growth. The World Wars and Swadeshi helped Indian capitalists (Tata, Birla, Walchand). By 1947 industry contributed only a small share of national income, showing the colonial nature of the economy.

The syllabus examines reforms under Cornwallis, Bentinck and Dalhousie as part of colonial modernisation. Administrative and institutional changes were introduced to strengthen governance while also producing wider social effects.

Modern education created new educated groups. The press expanded the public circulation of ideas, and a modern intelligentsia became increasingly active in debates on society, reform and politics.

Questions concerning the emancipation and education of women also became central to reform discussions.

Reforms: Cornwallis organised the civil service, judiciary (Cornwallis Code) and police and introduced the Permanent Settlement; Bentinck abolished sati, suppressed thuggee and female infanticide, introduced English education (1835) and opened some posts to Indians; Dalhousie introduced railways, telegraph, modern postal system, the Public Works Department and canals, and supported widow remarriage and Wood's Despatch. These measures aimed at efficient administration and economic exploitation, but also introduced new technologies and ideas.

Education and press: English education (Macaulay's Minute 1835, Wood's Despatch 1854, universities in 1857) produced a Western-educated class. The press (Bengal Gazette 1780, Sambad Kaumudi, Kesari, The Hindu, Amrita Bazar Patrika) spread reform and political ideas, despite repressive laws (Vernacular Press Act 1878). The intelligentsia - Rammohun Roy, Derozio and Young Bengal, Vidyasagar, Ranade, Naoroji, Tagore - led the 'Indian Renaissance', forming associations that led to the Congress.

Women: debates on sati, widow remarriage, child marriage and education led to laws (1829, 1856, 1891, 1929) and new schools. Women themselves (Pandita Ramabai, Savitribai Phule, Tarabai Shinde, Rokeya) began to write and organise. Historians debate whether colonial modernisation liberated or merely reshaped patriarchy; nationalist reformers tended to idealise women as guardians of tradition (Partha Chatterjee). Nevertheless, these changes laid the foundations of later women's movements.

The nineteenth century witnessed important movements such as the Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj, Ramakrishna Mission and Aligarh Movement. They differed in religious outlook and social programme but all responded to changing conditions in colonial India.

They addressed questions of religious reform, education, social customs and community development. Women's status and education also became important subjects of debate.

Their impact lay in stimulating public discussion and organised reform, although their influence differed across communities and regions.

Brahmo Samaj (Rammohun Roy, 1828): monotheism, rejection of idolatry, campaigns against sati and for women's rights and education; later leaders Debendranath Tagore and Keshab Chandra Sen; splits (1866, 1878). Prarthana Samaj (Bombay, 1867, Atmaram Pandurang, M. G. Ranade, R. G. Bhandarkar): inter-caste dining, widow remarriage, women's education. Arya Samaj (Dayanand Saraswati, 1875): 'Back to the Vedas', rejection of idolatry and caste by birth, shuddhi, DAV schools and Gurukuls. Theosophical Society (Madame Blavatsky and Colonel Olcott, 1875; headquarters at Adyar, Madras; later Annie Besant): revival of ancient religions and the Central Hindu College at Benares (1898).

Ramakrishna Mission (Vivekananda, 1897): universal religion, service to humanity, practical Vedanta, cultural pride. Aligarh Movement (Sir Syed Ahmad Khan): modern education for Muslims, rational interpretation of Islam, MAO College (1875). Other Muslim movements: the Deoband school (1866, orthodox), the Ahmadiyya movement (1889) and the Nadwatul Ulama. Sikh reform: the Singh Sabhas (1873) and the Akali movement (1920s) for control of gurdwaras. Lower caste movements: Phule's Satyashodhak Samaj (1873), Sree Narayana Dharma Paripalana Yogam (1903), Periyar's Self-Respect Movement and Ambedkar's campaigns.

Impact and evaluation: these movements encouraged rational thought, education and social reform, challenged some oppressive practices, and contributed to national self-respect and the rise of nationalism. However, they had a limited social base, some had revivalist and communal tendencies, and they often accepted aspects of caste and patriarchy. Historians debate whether they were a 'renaissance' or a response conditioned by colonial power.
Indian nationalism developed from political, economic and social changes under colonial rule, including modern education, communication, economic criticism and new public organisations.

Factors in the rise of nationalism: (1) political and administrative unification of India under British rule; (2) Western education and ideas of liberty, democracy and nationalism (from the French Revolution, Italian and Irish nationalism); (3) modern communications - railways, telegraph, post, press; (4) the economic critique of colonialism (Naoroji, Ranade, R. C. Dutt) showing exploitation and drain; (5) rediscovery of India's past by Orientalist scholars and Indian historians, giving pride; (6) socio-religious reform movements; (7) racial discrimination by the British (the Ilbert Bill controversy, 1883, when Europeans opposed Indian judges trying Europeans); and (8) reactionary policies of Lord Lytton (the Vernacular Press Act, Arms Act, Delhi Durbar during famine, lowering the ICS age limit).

Benedict Anderson called nations 'imagined communities' produced by print capitalism. Indian historians debate the nature of nationalism: nationalist historians see it as a mass anti-colonial movement; the Cambridge School (Anil Seal, John Gallagher) saw it as competition among elites for colonial patronage; Marxists emphasised class; and the Subaltern Studies school (Ranajit Guha) highlighted the autonomous politics of peasants and workers.
The Revolt grew from military, political, economic and social grievances. Its character varied regionally, but it became the greatest armed challenge to Company rule.

In 1857, sepoys at Meerut revolted on 10 May, marched to Delhi and proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar emperor of Hindustan. The revolt spread across north and central India. Leaders included Bakht Khan (Delhi), Nana Saheb, Tantia Tope and Azimullah Khan (Kanpur), Begum Hazrat Mahal and her son Birjis Qadr (Lucknow), Rani Lakshmibai (Jhansi), Kunwar Singh (Arrah, Bihar), Khan Bahadur Khan (Rohilkhand) and Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah (Faizabad). Peasants and taluqdars joined in Awadh and western Bihar.

The British, aided by Sikh and Gurkha troops and loyal princes, recaptured Delhi (September 1857), relieved Lucknow (1858) and crushed resistance by 1859. Causes included annexations, economic exploitation, social and religious fears and military grievances (greased cartridges). Its character is debated - a sepoy mutiny, feudal reaction, national war of independence (Savarkar) or popular uprising (Stokes, Guha). Its consequences included Crown rule, army reorganisation and a policy of alliance with princes and landlords.
The Act ended East India Company rule and transferred authority to the British Crown.

The Government of India Act 1858 (An Act for the Better Government of India), passed after the revolt, transferred the government of India from the East India Company to the British Crown. A new office of Secretary of State for India (a member of the British cabinet, the first being Lord Stanley) was created, assisted by a Council of India with fifteen members. The Board of Control and Court of Directors were abolished.

The Governor-General was given the title of Viceroy as the Crown's representative (Lord Canning was the first Viceroy). The Indian Civil Service was to be recruited by open competition under the Secretary of State. Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1 November 1858, read at Allahabad) announced the end of territorial expansion, respect for princes' rights, religious toleration, equal opportunities in government service regardless of race or religion (rarely fulfilled), and an amnesty.
These Acts introduced limited changes in legislative councils and gradually widened Indian participation without establishing responsible government.

Indian Councils Act 1861: added between six and twelve 'additional members' to the Viceroy's Executive Council for legislative purposes, of whom at least half were non-officials; some Indians were nominated (such as the Raja of Benares, the Maharaja of Patiala and Sir Dinkar Rao). Legislative councils were restored in Bombay and Madras and created for Bengal (1862), the North-Western Provinces (1886) and Punjab (1897). It introduced the portfolio system (Canning) and allowed the Viceroy to issue ordinances in emergencies. The councils were purely advisory.

Indian Councils Act 1892: increased the number of additional members (10-16 in the central council), introduced an indirect, limited election principle (members could be recommended by universities, district boards, municipalities, chambers of commerce and zamindars), and allowed members to discuss the budget and ask questions (but not supplementary questions or vote). It was a response to Congress demands but fell far short of representative government. Gokhale and others used these councils to criticise government policy.
The Morley-Minto reforms enlarged legislative councils and introduced separate electorates for Muslims.

The Indian Councils Act of 1909 is known as the Morley-Minto Reforms, after Secretary of State John Morley and Viceroy Lord Minto. It increased the size of the legislative councils (up to 60 additional members in the Imperial Legislative Council and up to 50 in larger provinces), with a non-official majority in provincial councils; members could ask supplementary questions, move resolutions on the budget and matters of public interest, though the government was not bound by them.

It introduced separate electorates for Muslims, in which only Muslims voted for Muslim candidates, after the Simla Deputation (1906) and the formation of the Muslim League. An Indian, S. P. Sinha, was appointed to the Viceroy's Executive Council. The reforms aimed to win the support of the moderates and Muslims and to isolate the extremists; nationalists saw separate electorates as a 'divide and rule' strategy that laid the foundation of communal politics. Minto is sometimes called the 'father of communal electorates'.
The Act introduced dyarchy in the provinces and expanded legislatures, while real colonial control remained strong.

The Government of India Act 1919 implemented the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms, following Secretary of State Edwin Montagu's declaration of August 1917 promising 'the progressive realisation of responsible government in India'. In the provinces, it introduced dyarchy: 'transferred' subjects (education, health, local self-government, agriculture) were placed under Indian ministers responsible to the legislature, while 'reserved' subjects (law and order, finance, land revenue, irrigation) remained under the Governor and his executive council.

At the centre, it created a bicameral legislature - the Council of State and the Legislative Assembly - with an elected majority, but the Viceroy retained full control and could certify laws. It expanded separate electorates to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans; extended franchise to about 10 percent of adult males on property qualifications; and created a Public Service Commission (1926). It also separated central and provincial budgets. The Congress rejected it as inadequate, especially after the Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh.
The Act introduced provincial autonomy and proposed an all-India federation that did not fully come into operation.

The Government of India Act 1935 was based on the Simon Commission report, the Round Table Conferences and the White Paper (1933). It was the longest act passed by the British Parliament until then (321 sections). It proposed an All-India Federation of British provinces and princely states, which never came into operation because princes refused to join. It divided powers into three lists - federal, provincial and concurrent - and introduced dyarchy at the centre (on paper).

It abolished dyarchy in the provinces and introduced provincial autonomy, with responsible governments under Indian ministers (but governors had special powers). It extended separate electorates to depressed classes (with the modifications of the Poona Pact), women and labour; extended franchise to about 14 percent of the population; established a Federal Court (1937) and the Reserve Bank of India; separated Burma from India and created Sindh and Orissa as new provinces. Elections in 1937 led to Congress ministries in eight provinces. Many features of the Act were later adopted in the Constitution of India.
Founded in 1885, the Congress became the main all-India organisation of the national movement.

The Indian National Congress was founded on 28 December 1885 at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay, with 72 delegates. A. O. Hume, a retired British civil servant, helped organise it; W. C. Bonnerjee was its first president. Historians once argued (the 'safety valve' theory, from William Wedderburn's biography of Hume) that it was founded to provide a safe outlet for Indian discontent; Bipan Chandra argued instead that Indian leaders used Hume as a 'lightning conductor' to avoid government suspicion.

The Congress met annually in different cities, passed resolutions and became the main platform of the national movement. Its phases: Moderate (1885-1905), Extremist (1905-1918), and Gandhian (1919-1947). Major sessions include Calcutta 1906 (swaraj demanded under Naoroji), Surat 1907 (split), Lucknow 1916 (reunion and Lucknow Pact), Nagpur 1920 (non-cooperation), Lahore 1929 (Purna Swaraj), Karachi 1931 (Fundamental Rights) and Haripura 1938 and Tripuri 1939 (Subhas Bose). After independence, it became India's ruling party.
Moderates relied largely on constitutional agitation, while Extremists supported stronger mobilisation, swadeshi and boycott.

Moderates (1885-1905): Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, Surendranath Banerjea, Gokhale, W. C. Bonnerjee, Badruddin Tyabji. Beliefs: faith in British justice and liberalism; gradual constitutional reform; methods of petitions, resolutions, speeches and delegations; demands for Indianisation of services, expanded councils, reduced military expenditure, lower land revenue, protection of industry and civil rights. Achievements: economic critique of colonialism (drain theory), political education and national unity.

Extremists (1905-1918): Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, Lala Lajpat Rai, Aurobindo Ghosh. Beliefs: swaraj as a right; distrust of British intentions; pride in Indian culture; mass mobilisation; methods of swadeshi, boycott, national education and passive resistance. The two groups split at Surat (1907) and reunited at Lucknow (1916). Historians note that both contributed - the moderates laid foundations and the extremists broadened the movement's social base.
The 1905 partition of Bengal generated a powerful anti-partition movement based on boycott, swadeshi and national education.

Partition (announced July 1905, effective 16 October 1905) divided Bengal into Western Bengal (with Bihar and Odisha) and Eastern Bengal and Assam (capital Dacca). The British claimed administrative reasons, but the aim was to weaken the Bengali nationalist movement and to create a Muslim-majority province to divide Hindus and Muslims. Protests began immediately: 16 October was a day of mourning, people tied rakhis, and Tagore wrote 'Amar Sonar Bangla'.

The Swadeshi movement (declared 7 August 1905) included boycott of British goods, swadeshi enterprises (textile mills, Bengal Chemicals, Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company), national education (National Council of Education, 1906), samitis, cultural revival and later passive resistance. Its spread to other parts of India, extremist leadership and the 1906 Calcutta session's demand for swaraj marked a new phase. Repression, the Surat split, communal divisions and the turn to revolutionary terrorism (Alipore Bomb Case, 1908) ended it by 1908. The partition was annulled in 1911.
The movement demanded self-government and helped revive nationalist politics during the First World War.

Tilak, released in 1914, and Annie Besant, an Irish theosophist, founded Home Rule Leagues in 1916 - Tilak's in April (Belgaum) and Besant's in September (Madras) - demanding self-government within the British Empire on the Irish model. They organised meetings, discussion groups, libraries and newspapers, and recruited members among youth and in new areas such as Gujarat and Sindh.

The movement revived nationalist politics at a time when the Congress was weak, contributed to the reunion of moderates and extremists and the Congress-League Lucknow Pact (1916), and prepared the ground for Gandhian mass movements. Besant's arrest (June 1917) caused protests, and she was released in September 1917 and elected Congress president for 1917. The Montagu Declaration (August 1917) was partly a response. The movement declined by 1919 due to Tilak's visit to England, Besant's acceptance of the reforms and the rise of Gandhi.
The Congress Socialist Party and Communist Party of India represented important socialist and communist currents in the freedom struggle.

Background: the Russian Revolution (1917) inspired Indian socialists; the Great Depression showed the crisis of capitalism. M. N. Roy founded the CPI in exile at Tashkent (1920); communist groups in India (S. A. Dange in Bombay, Muzaffar Ahmad in Calcutta, Singaravelu in Madras, Ghulam Hussain in Lahore) held the Kanpur conference (1925). Communists organised workers (the Workers' and Peasants' Parties, the Girni Kamgar Union in Bombay) and led strikes; the Meerut Conspiracy Case (1929-1933) imprisoned 31 leaders. The CPI was banned in 1934.

The Congress Socialist Party (1934, Patna/Bombay) was formed by Jayaprakash Narayan, Acharya Narendra Dev, Minoo Masani, Ram Manohar Lohia and others within Congress. Nehru's speeches (Lucknow 1936) emphasised socialism. The All India Kisan Sabha (1936, Swami Sahajanand Saraswati) and the All India Students' Federation (1936) were formed. The left pushed for land reform, workers' rights and complete independence, but was divided. The CPI's support for the British war effort after 1941 isolated it during Quit India; later it led the Tebhaga and Telangana movements.
Both became major revolutionary figures. Bhagat Singh connected revolutionary action with radical political thought, while Surya Sen led the Chittagong Armoury Raid.

Bhagat Singh: born 1907 in Punjab; joined the Naujawan Bharat Sabha (1926); co-founded the HSRA (1928) with Chandrashekhar Azad, which aimed at a socialist republic; killed Saunders (1928) to avenge Lajpat Rai; threw bombs in the Central Legislative Assembly with B. K. Dutt (8 April 1929) to protest the Public Safety Bill and Trade Disputes Bill, raising the slogan 'Inquilab Zindabad'. His hunger strike in jail for political prisoners' rights gained national attention. He was hanged with Rajguru and Sukhdev on 23 March 1931, despite appeals. His writings ('Why I am an Atheist') show a commitment to socialism, rationalism and secularism.

Surya Sen: a schoolteacher from Chittagong, he led the Indian Republican Army. On 18 April 1930, his group raided two armouries, cut communications and declared a provisional government. At Jalalabad hills (22 April 1930), they fought British troops, and several young revolutionaries were killed. Kalpana Dutta and Pritilata Waddedar joined later actions. Surya Sen was betrayed, captured in 1933 and hanged on 12 January 1934. Revolutionary nationalism inspired youth and showed courage, but Gandhi and the Congress disapproved of violence.
The syllabus examines the Muslim League and Hindu Mahasabha in relation to the growth of communal political organisation.

Communal consciousness - the belief that people of one religion have common political, economic and social interests opposed to those of other religions - grew from the late nineteenth century. Contributing factors included the British policy of 'divide and rule' (separate electorates from 1909, the Communal Award of 1932), the economic backwardness of Muslims and competition for jobs among the educated middle classes, revivalist movements (cow protection, shuddhi, tabligh), and a communal reading of history (portraying medieval India as Muslim tyranny).

The Muslim League (1906) demanded separate electorates and safeguards; after the 1937 elections, Jinnah reorganised it as a mass party, and the Lahore Resolution (1940) demanded Pakistan. The Hindu Mahasabha (1915) under Malaviya, Lajpat Rai, B. S. Moonje and Savarkar promoted Hindu unity and Hindutva; the RSS (1925) built a cadre organisation. Communal riots increased in the 1920s and 1940s, culminating in the Direct Action Day (1946) and the violence of Partition.
Gandhi's satyagraha emphasised truth, non-violence and disciplined resistance against injustice.

Satyagraha (from 'satya', truth, and 'agraha', insistence or firmness) was developed by Gandhi in South Africa (from 1906) against the Asiatic Registration Act and racial laws. It means resisting injustice through non-violence (ahimsa), willingness to suffer, refusal to obey unjust laws, and an appeal to the conscience of the opponent rather than hatred. A satyagrahi must be truthful, fearless, non-violent and disciplined.

Methods include non-cooperation, civil disobedience, hartal (strikes), boycott, fasting, picketing and constructive work. Gandhi distinguished it from 'passive resistance', which he saw as a weapon of the weak that could include violence. His ideas drew on the Gita, Jainism, Christianity (the Sermon on the Mount), Tolstoy, Thoreau and Ruskin. Satyagraha influenced civil rights movements worldwide, including Martin Luther King Jr. and Nelson Mandela.
The 1919 Rowlatt Act allowed extraordinary repressive measures and provoked widespread opposition.

The Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act (1919), based on the report of the Sedition Committee headed by Justice S. A. T. Rowlatt, allowed the government to imprison people without trial for up to two years, to try cases in special courts without juries and appeals, and to restrict the press. Indians called it the 'Black Act' - 'no vakil, no daleel, no appeal'. All Indian members of the Imperial Legislative Council opposed it; Jinnah, Madan Mohan Malaviya and Mazhar-ul-Haq resigned.

Gandhi formed the Satyagraha Sabha and called a nationwide hartal on 6 April 1919 - his first all-India movement. There was violence in some places, and Gandhi was arrested. In Amritsar, the arrest of Dr Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr Satyapal led to protests. On 13 April 1919 (Baisakhi), General Reginald Dyer ordered troops to fire without warning on a peaceful crowd at Jallianwala Bagh, killing hundreds (official figure 379; Indian estimates over 1,000). Tagore returned his knighthood. The Hunter Committee's inquiry was seen as a whitewash. These events turned many moderates against British rule.
The Khilafat and Non-Cooperation movements brought large-scale mobilisation against British rule in the early 1920s.

Khilafat: after the First World War, the Treaty of Sevres (1920) dismembered the Ottoman Empire, threatening the position of the Sultan as Caliph (Khalifa), the religious head of Sunni Muslims. Indian Muslims, led by the Ali brothers (Mohammad Ali and Shaukat Ali), Maulana Azad, Hakim Ajmal Khan and Hasrat Mohani, formed the Khilafat Committee (1919). Gandhi saw an opportunity for Hindu-Muslim unity and supported it.

The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-1922) combined the Khilafat issue, the Punjab wrongs (Jallianwala Bagh) and swaraj. It included the surrender of titles, boycott of government schools, courts, councils and foreign cloth, the burning of foreign cloth, promotion of khadi, and national institutions. C. R. Das, Motilal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel and Rajendra Prasad gave up their legal practice. It spread to peasants (Awadh Kisan Sabha), tribals (Andhra's Alluri Sitarama Raju, though independently) and workers, with the Moplah rebellion in Malabar (1921) becoming communal. Gandhi withdrew it after Chauri Chaura (February 1922). The Khilafat issue ended when Turkey abolished the caliphate (1924).
Civil Disobedience involved deliberate non-violent violation of colonial laws. The Salt March became its best-known action.

After the Lahore Congress (1929) declared Purna Swaraj, Gandhi presented eleven demands to Viceroy Irwin, including abolition of the salt tax, reduction of land revenue and military expenditure, release of political prisoners and protective tariffs. When they were rejected, he began the Dandi March (12 March - 6 April 1930), breaking the salt law at Dandi. Salt was chosen because it affected everyone, rich and poor.

The movement spread across India: salt satyagraha at Dharasana (where peaceful volunteers led by Sarojini Naidu were brutally beaten, as reported by the American journalist Webb Miller), boycott of foreign cloth and liquor, no-tax campaigns, forest satyagrahas, Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan's Red Shirts (and the Peshawar firing; the Garhwali soldiers under Chandra Singh Garhwali refused to fire on crowds), and Rani Gaidinliu's resistance in the north-east. The Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 1931) led to Gandhi's participation in the Second Round Table Conference, which failed. The movement was renewed in 1932 and withdrawn in 1934. It marked greater participation of women, peasants and merchants.
Launched in 1942, Quit India demanded an immediate end to British rule and produced widespread resistance.

Causes: the failure of the Cripps Mission; the threat of Japanese invasion after the fall of Singapore, Malaya and Burma (1942); wartime shortages and price rises; and British discrimination during the evacuation from Burma. The All India Congress Committee passed the Quit India resolution at Gowalia Tank, Bombay, on 8 August 1942. Gandhi's speech called on Indians to 'Do or Die'.

On 9 August, Gandhi and Congress leaders were arrested; Gandhi was held at the Aga Khan Palace in Pune, where his wife Kasturba and secretary Mahadev Desai died. Without leaders, people attacked symbols of British authority: railway stations, police stations, post offices and telegraph lines; parallel governments were set up in Ballia (Chittu Pandey), Tamluk (Midnapore) and Satara (Nana Patil). Underground leaders included Jayaprakash Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia, Aruna Asaf Ali, Sucheta Kripalani and Usha Mehta. The British used massive force, including aerial machine-gunning. The movement was crushed by the end of 1942, but it showed that India would no longer accept British rule.
Swarajists entered colonial legislatures to obstruct and challenge government from within.

After the withdrawal of the Non-Cooperation Movement, the Congress was divided between 'no-changers' (Vallabhbhai Patel, Rajendra Prasad, C. Rajagopalachari), who wanted to continue Gandhi's constructive programme and boycott of the councils, and 'pro-changers', led by C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru, who wanted to contest elections and wreck the councils from within. Das and Motilal formed the Swaraj Party (Congress-Khilafat Swaraj Party) in January 1923.

In the 1923 elections, the Swarajists won many seats, especially in the Central Legislative Assembly and Bengal and the Central Provinces. They obstructed government business, defeated budgets, passed resolutions demanding self-government and civil liberties, and exposed the hollowness of the 1919 reforms. Vithalbhai Patel became the first Indian President (speaker) of the Central Legislative Assembly (1925). The party declined after C. R. Das's death (1925) and divisions over cooperating with the government, but it kept political activity alive during the 1920s.
The Royal Indian Navy Mutiny of 1946 showed serious discontent among naval ratings in the final phase of colonial rule.

The mutiny began on 18 February 1946 when ratings of HMIS Talwar, a signals training establishment in Bombay, went on hunger strike against bad food, racial abuse by British officers, low pay and poor conditions; the arrest of B. C. Dutt, who had written 'Quit India' on the ship, was a trigger. It spread to Castle Barracks, Fort Barracks and 22 ships in Bombay harbour, then to Karachi, Calcutta, Madras, Visakhapatnam and other naval bases; about 20,000 ratings joined. A Naval Central Strike Committee led by M. S. Khan was formed.

Workers and students in Bombay held a general strike in support, and street battles with police and troops left over 200 dead. The Congress and League leaders did not support the mutiny; Vallabhbhai Patel and Jinnah advised surrender, which took place on 23 February. Only the Communists supported the strike. The mutiny, along with the INA trials and unrest in the air force and army, convinced the British that they could no longer rely on Indian armed forces.
The INA sought to fight British rule militarily and became closely associated with Subhas Chandra Bose.

Phase one: Captain Mohan Singh, with Japanese support, formed the INA in 1942 from Indian prisoners captured at Singapore; disagreements with the Japanese led to its dissolution. Phase two: Subhas Chandra Bose, who had resigned as Congress president (1939), formed the Forward Bloc, escaped from house arrest in Calcutta (January 1941) and reached Germany, where he formed the Free India Centre and the Indian Legion. He travelled by submarine to Southeast Asia (1943) and took leadership of the INA and the Indian Independence League from Rash Behari Bose.

Bose formed the Provisional Government of Free India (21 October 1943), which declared war on Britain and the USA and was recognised by the Axis powers. The INA had brigades named after Gandhi, Nehru, Azad and Bose, and the Rani of Jhansi women's regiment. It fought in Arakan and in the Imphal-Kohima campaign (1944) and briefly raised the Indian flag at Moirang in Manipur (April 1944). After Japan's defeat, the INA surrendered; Bose reportedly died in a plane crash at Taipei (18 August 1945). The Red Fort trials (1945-1946), defended by Bhulabhai Desai, Nehru and others, triggered nationwide protests and influenced the armed forces.
Opposition to the Simon Commission was followed by Indian efforts to formulate constitutional proposals in the Nehru Report.

Simon Commission: appointed in November 1927 under Sir John Simon to review the 1919 Act, it included Clement Attlee but no Indians, which Indians saw as an insult. When it arrived in February 1928, it was greeted with hartals, black flags and 'Simon Go Back' slogans. Lala Lajpat Rai was fatally injured in a police lathi-charge at Lahore. The Commission's report (1930) recommended provincial autonomy and federalism but not dominion status.

Nehru Report: in response to Lord Birkenhead's challenge, the All Parties Conference appointed a committee under Motilal Nehru (with Jawaharlal Nehru as secretary) whose report (August 1928) proposed dominion status, a parliamentary system with responsible government, universal adult suffrage, nineteen fundamental rights (including equal rights for women), joint electorates with reservation of seats for minorities and linguistic provinces. The Muslim League under Jinnah rejected it and issued his 'Fourteen Points' (1929). Young radicals (Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Bose) formed the Independence for India League, and the Congress gave Britain one year to accept the report, after which it declared Purna Swaraj (1929).
These initiatives attempted to address constitutional deadlock and the transfer of power during the 1940s.

Cripps Mission (March 1942): Sir Stafford Cripps offered dominion status after the war, a constituent assembly with representatives of provinces and princely states, the right of provinces to opt out, and Indian participation in an expanded Executive Council (but defence remained under British control). Congress and the League rejected it, leading to the Quit India Movement.

Wavell Plan and Simla Conference (June-July 1945): Lord Wavell proposed an Indian Executive Council (except the Viceroy and Commander-in-Chief) with parity between caste Hindus and Muslims. It failed because Jinnah insisted that only the League could nominate Muslim members. Cabinet Mission (March-June 1946): Pethick-Lawrence, Cripps and A. V. Alexander proposed a three-tier federal structure (Union, groups of provinces and provinces), grouping provinces into A (Hindu majority), B (north-west Muslim majority) and C (Bengal and Assam), a Constituent Assembly elected by provincial assemblies, and an interim government; it rejected the demand for a separate Pakistan. Disputes over grouping led the League to withdraw and call Direct Action Day (16 August 1946).
The 1947 plan accepted partition and provided the immediate political framework for the transfer of power.

Lord Mountbatten arrived as Viceroy in March 1947 with instructions to transfer power by June 1948. After consulting leaders and facing escalating communal violence, he proposed the 3 June Plan: partition of India into India and Pakistan; the provincial legislative assemblies of Punjab and Bengal would decide on partition (both voted to partition); a referendum in the North-West Frontier Province (which joined Pakistan) and in Sylhet district of Assam (which joined East Pakistan); Sindh and Baluchistan would decide; and boundary commissions would demarcate the frontiers.

Princely states could join either dominion. Power would be transferred on the basis of dominion status. The date was advanced to 15 August 1947. Nehru, Patel, Jinnah and Baldev Singh accepted the plan; Gandhi accepted it reluctantly. The Radcliffe Line was announced on 17 August 1947. The haste of partition contributed to the massive violence and refugee crisis.
The Act created the two Dominions of India and Pakistan and legally ended British rule.

The Indian Independence Act (18 July 1947) created the independent dominions of India and Pakistan from 15 August 1947 (Pakistan celebrated on 14 August). It abolished the office of Secretary of State for India and the British government's responsibility for India; ended paramountcy over princely states; empowered the Constituent Assemblies to frame constitutions and act as legislatures; provided for Governors-General appointed by the Crown on the advice of the dominion cabinets; and allowed the 1935 Act to function as the interim constitution until new constitutions were adopted.

Mountbatten became the first Governor-General of India (succeeded by C. Rajagopalachari, the only Indian Governor-General, in 1948), and Jinnah became Governor-General of Pakistan. Nehru became the first Prime Minister. India became a republic on 26 January 1950, ending its dominion status.
B. R. Ambedkar played a major role in constitution-making, especially as Chairman of the Drafting Committee.

The Constituent Assembly, elected indirectly by provincial assemblies in 1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan, first met on 9 December 1946; Dr Sachchidananda Sinha was temporary chairman and Dr Rajendra Prasad was elected President. Nehru's Objectives Resolution (13 December 1946) set out the principles. After partition, the Assembly had 299 members. Committees included the Union Powers Committee and Union Constitution Committee (Nehru), the Provincial Constitution Committee and the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities (Patel).

B. R. Ambedkar (1891-1956), a Dalit scholar and leader who had founded the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924), led the Mahad satyagraha (1927) and burned the Manusmriti, and debated with Gandhi on separate electorates (Poona Pact, 1932), was appointed Chairman of the Drafting Committee (29 August 1947). He is known as the 'chief architect' of the Constitution. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950. Ambedkar ensured fundamental rights, abolition of untouchability (Article 17) and reservations for Scheduled Castes and Tribes; he became India's first Law Minister.
After independence, princely states were integrated into the Indian Union through negotiation, accession and, in some cases, political pressure.

At independence, there were about 565 princely states covering about 40 percent of India's area. With the lapse of paramountcy, they could theoretically become independent. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, as Home Minister and Minister of States, with his secretary V. P. Menon, persuaded most rulers to sign the Instrument of Accession (surrendering defence, external affairs and communications) and later the Merger Agreements, by appealing to patriotism and offering privy purses and privileges (abolished in 1971).

Problems: Junagadh (Muslim ruler, Hindu majority) acceded to Pakistan, but a plebiscite in February 1948 confirmed its integration with India. Hyderabad, under the Nizam, sought independence; the Razakars' violence led to 'Operation Polo' (police action, September 1948). Kashmir's Maharaja Hari Singh acceded to India in October 1947 after an invasion by tribesmen from Pakistan, leading to the first India-Pakistan war. Manipur and Tripura were integrated in 1949. Patel is called the 'Iron Man of India' for this achievement.

sections.title: Rise of Nationalism and Constitutional Development

blocks.text:
Nationalism grew from colonial economic criticism, modern education, communications, public associations and increasing political consciousness. The Revolt of 1857 was an early major challenge to colonial rule.

After 1857, the Government of India Act transferred power from the Company to the Crown. Later Acts of 1861, 1892, 1909, 1919 and 1935 gradually changed councils and provincial government but retained British supremacy.

These limited reforms encouraged further demands for representative and responsible government.

Rise of nationalism: the unification of India by British administration, communications and English education; the economic critique of colonialism; Orientalist research and the rediscovery of the past; socio-religious reform; the press; racial discrimination (the Ilbert Bill controversy); and Lytton's reactionary measures. Pre-Congress associations led to the founding of the Congress in 1885. The 1857 revolt, though not nationalist in the modern sense, became a symbol of resistance.

Constitutional development: the Government of India Act 1858 (Crown rule); the Indian Councils Acts of 1861 (nominated Indians in councils) and 1892 (indirect election, budget discussion); the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909 (enlarged councils, separate electorates); the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms of 1919 (dyarchy in provinces, bicameral central legislature); and the Government of India Act 1935 (provincial autonomy, proposed federation, Federal Court).

Analysis: each reform was a response to nationalist pressure, but each was designed to maintain British control - by giving limited representation, retaining executive power, using separate electorates to divide communities and allying with princes and landlords. The limited nature of reforms intensified demands for full self-government, while institutions such as legislatures, elections and federalism became part of India's political experience and influenced the Constitution of 1950.

sections.title: Congress, Swadeshi and Other Political Currents

blocks.text:
The Indian National Congress became the principal national organisation. Moderates initially favoured constitutional agitation, while Extremists advocated more assertive methods.

The Partition of Bengal stimulated the Swadeshi Movement. Home Rule later revived the demand for self-government. Leftist organisations added socialist and communist perspectives, while Bhagat Singh and Surya Sen represented revolutionary nationalism.

The Muslim League and Hindu Mahasabha are included in the syllabus as part of the development of communal political consciousness.

Congress and its phases: founded in 1885 with Moderate leadership (Naoroji, Gokhale, Mehta, Banerjea), who used constitutional methods and developed the economic critique; Extremists (Lal-Bal-Pal, Aurobindo) demanded swaraj and mass action. The Surat split (1907) and the Lucknow reunion (1916) marked changes. The Swadeshi movement (1905-1908) against the partition of Bengal used boycott, swadeshi, national education and samitis, spreading nationalism widely. The Home Rule Leagues (1916) revived nationalism during the war.

Left and revolutionary currents: revolutionary groups (Anushilan Samiti, Jugantar, Abhinav Bharat, Ghadar Party, HRA/HSRA) used armed action; Bhagat Singh linked revolution with socialism; Surya Sen led the Chittagong raid. The CPI (1920/1925) and CSP (1934) organised workers and peasants and pushed the Congress leftward. Communal politics: the Muslim League (1906), separate electorates (1909), the Lucknow Pact (1916), the Hindu Mahasabha and RSS, Jinnah's Fourteen Points (1929) and the Lahore Resolution (1940).

Analysis: the national movement contained diverse currents - liberal constitutionalism, assertive nationalism, revolutionary violence, socialism and communal politics. The Congress tried to act as an umbrella organisation, but communal divisions deepened, especially after 1937, leading to Partition. Each current contributed to the political awakening of Indians and the final achievement of independence.

Gandhi transformed the freedom movement through satyagraha and mass non-violent mobilisation. The Rowlatt agitation, Khilafat and Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience and Quit India brought large numbers of Indians into anti-colonial politics.

Swarajists used legislatures as a field of political struggle. The INA attempted armed resistance from outside British India, while the RIN Mutiny showed discontent within the colonial armed forces.

Together these developments weakened the legitimacy and stability of British rule.

Gandhi's leadership: satyagraha and non-violence; local campaigns (Champaran, Kheda, Ahmedabad); the Rowlatt satyagraha (1919) and Jallianwala Bagh; Khilafat and Non-Cooperation (1920-1922), withdrawn after Chauri Chaura; constructive programme and the Swarajists' council entry (1923-1926); Civil Disobedience (1930-1934) with the Dandi March, Gandhi-Irwin Pact and Round Table Conferences; and Quit India (1942) with 'Do or Die'. Gandhian movements brought peasants, women, workers, students and merchants into the national struggle and gave the Congress a mass base.

Swarajists: C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru entered legislatures in 1923 to oppose the government from within, keeping political interest alive. Armed challenges: the INA under Subhas Bose fought with Japanese support (Imphal-Kohima, 1944); the INA trials (1945-1946) united Indians in sympathy. The RIN Mutiny (1946) and unrest in the air force and police showed the collapse of loyalty of Indian forces.

Evaluation: Gandhian non-violence and mass mobilisation eroded the moral legitimacy of British rule, while armed challenges and military unrest threatened its physical basis. Britain's weakened economy after the war, American pressure and the Labour government's attitude also contributed. Historians debate the relative importance of these factors, but agree that the combination made British rule unsustainable by 1946-1947.

The Simon Commission and Nehru Report intensified constitutional debate. During the 1940s, the Cripps Mission, Wavell Plan and Cabinet Mission tried unsuccessfully to secure an agreed political settlement.

The Mountbatten Plan accepted partition, and the Indian Independence Act 1947 created India and Pakistan. Constitution-making continued through the Constituent Assembly, where B. R. Ambedkar played a central drafting role.

The new Indian government also faced the major task of integrating princely states into the Union.

Constitutional negotiations: the Simon Commission (1927) and its boycott; the Nehru Report (1928) and Jinnah's Fourteen Points; the Round Table Conferences (1930-1932) and the Communal Award (1932), modified by the Poona Pact; the 1935 Act and provincial elections (1937); the August Offer (1940); the Cripps Mission (1942); the Wavell Plan and Simla Conference (1945); the 1945-1946 elections; and the Cabinet Mission (1946), its grouping scheme and interim government. Repeated failures resulted from the Congress-League conflict and British policies.

Transfer of power: Direct Action Day and communal riots (Calcutta, Noakhali, Bihar, Punjab), Attlee's announcement (February 1947), Mountbatten's 3 June Plan, the Indian Independence Act (July 1947), Partition and independence (15 August 1947). Partition caused perhaps 10-15 million refugees and hundreds of thousands to a million deaths; Gandhi worked for peace in Noakhali and Calcutta and was assassinated on 30 January 1948.

Constitution and integration: the Constituent Assembly (1946-1949), with Rajendra Prasad as President and B. R. Ambedkar as Chairman of the Drafting Committee, framed a Constitution establishing a sovereign democratic republic with fundamental rights, directive principles, federalism, parliamentary government and protections for minorities and Scheduled Castes and Tribes; it came into force on 26 January 1950. Sardar Patel and V. P. Menon integrated over 560 princely states through the Instrument of Accession, merger agreements and, in Hyderabad, police action. These steps consolidated India as a nation-state.
The rise of the Ottoman Empire changed the political and commercial world of the eastern Mediterranean and formed an important background to European expansion.

The Ottomans, a Turkish dynasty founded by Osman I (c. 1300) in Anatolia, expanded into the Balkans, captured Constantinople in 1453 under Mehmed II (renaming it Istanbul) and ended the Byzantine Empire. Under Selim I they conquered Syria, Egypt and the holy cities of Arabia (1516-1517), and under Suleiman the Magnificent (1520-1566) they conquered Hungary (Mohács, 1526), besieged Vienna (1529) and dominated the eastern Mediterranean.

The Ottoman control of eastern Mediterranean and overland trade routes increased the cost of Asian goods for Europeans, encouraging Portuguese and Spanish searches for new sea routes. The Ottomans had a strong army (the Janissaries), artillery and a navy; they were defeated at sea at Lepanto (1571) and before Vienna (1683). Historians now see the Ottoman Empire as part of the early modern European world, not merely as an outside threat.
Catalunya, Venice and Genoa developed sea-based commercial and colonial networks before the great Atlantic empires.

Before the Atlantic empires, Mediterranean powers built commercial empires. Venice controlled trade with the eastern Mediterranean and Black Sea, held colonies such as Crete, Cyprus and parts of Dalmatia and Greece, and dominated the spice trade through Alexandria. Genoa had colonies in the Black Sea (Caffa in Crimea) and the Aegean (Chios), traded in grain, alum and slaves, and its bankers later financed Spanish expansion. The Crown of Aragon and Catalan merchants (Barcelona) controlled Sicily, Sardinia and Naples and traded across the western Mediterranean.

These powers developed techniques later used in the Atlantic: chartered companies, colonial plantations (Venetian sugar in Cyprus and Crete, using slave labour), maritime insurance, banking, navigation and ship design. Italian sailors and financiers such as Christopher Columbus (a Genoese) and Amerigo Vespucci (a Florentine) played major roles in later voyages.
Shortages of precious metals encouraged European merchants and states to search for new sources of gold and new trade routes.

Late medieval Europe suffered a shortage of gold and silver (bullion famine) because it imported more from Asia than it exported, paying with precious metals. West African gold from the empires of Ghana, Mali (Mansa Musa's famous pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 displayed huge wealth) and Songhai was carried by trans-Saharan caravans to North African ports controlled by Muslim merchants.

The Portuguese wanted direct access to this gold by sea. After capturing Ceuta in North Africa (1415), they explored the West African coast, established the trading fort of Elmina (São Jorge da Mina, 1482) on the Gold Coast (Ghana), and traded for gold, ivory, pepper and slaves. The search for gold, along with spices and Christian zeal (the legend of Prester John), motivated exploration.
Improvements in ships, navigation and maritime knowledge made longer oceanic voyages increasingly possible.

The Portuguese developed the caravel, a small, fast ship with lateen (triangular) sails that could sail against the wind, and later the larger carrack (nau) for long voyages and cargo. Navigation was improved by the magnetic compass (from China), the astrolabe and quadrant for measuring latitude by the sun or the Pole Star, portolan charts and better maps, and knowledge of Atlantic wind systems (the volta do mar, sailing far into the Atlantic to catch favourable winds).

Prince Henry the Navigator (1394-1460) sponsored voyages along the African coast and gathered navigators, mapmakers and shipbuilders. Ships were armed with cannons, giving Europeans a military advantage at sea. The printing press spread geographic knowledge (Ptolemy's 'Geography'). These innovations made oceanic voyages possible.
Portuguese maritime exploration created a direct sea route linking Europe to the Indian Ocean.

The Portuguese gradually advanced along the African coast: Gil Eanes rounded Cape Bojador (1434), Diogo Cão reached the Congo (1482), and Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope (1488). Vasco da Gama sailed from Lisbon in 1497, rounded the Cape, visited Mozambique, Mombasa and Malindi, where a Gujarati or Arab pilot guided him across the Arabian Sea, and reached Calicut on 20 May 1498. He returned with spices that earned huge profits.

Pedro Álvares Cabral (1500), on the way to India, reached Brazil. The Portuguese established the Estado da India with bases at Cochin, Goa (1510), Malacca (1511), Hormuz (1515), Diu, Colombo and Macau (1557), and controlled the spice trade through force (the cartaz system). The direct sea route reduced the importance of Venice and the Mediterranean routes and began European maritime dominance in Asia.
Spanish conquest established a vast empire in the Americas and transferred enormous wealth and resources into European networks.

Christopher Columbus, sponsored by Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, sailed west to reach Asia and landed in the Bahamas in October 1492, then reached Cuba and Hispaniola. The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided the newly discovered lands between Spain and Portugal. Spanish conquistadors conquered large empires: Hernán Cortés conquered the Aztec Empire of Mexico (1519-1521), capturing Tenochtitlan with the help of indigenous allies; Francisco Pizarro conquered the Inca Empire of Peru (1532-1533), capturing Atahualpa.

Reasons for success included steel weapons, guns, horses, alliances with indigenous enemies of the Aztecs and Incas, and especially European diseases (smallpox), which killed perhaps 90 percent of the indigenous population. The Spanish established the encomienda system of forced labour, exploited silver mines such as Potosí (Bolivia, 1545) and Zacatecas (Mexico), and converted indigenous people to Christianity. Bartolomé de las Casas protested against the cruelty. The 'Columbian Exchange' (Alfred Crosby) transferred crops (maize, potatoes, tomatoes, tobacco), animals and diseases between the hemispheres.
The Renaissance was a cultural and intellectual movement marked by renewed engagement with classical learning, humanism and new artistic forms.

The Renaissance ('rebirth') began in fourteenth-century Italy and spread to northern Europe in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. The Swiss historian Jacob Burckhardt ('The Civilization of the Renaissance in Italy', 1860) saw it as the birth of modern individualism. Causes of its Italian origin include wealthy city-states (Florence, Venice, Milan, Rome) with patrons such as the Medici and the popes, the survival of Roman remains, contact with Byzantium and the Islamic world, and the arrival of Greek scholars after 1453.

Art: realism, perspective (Brunelleschi), anatomy and naturalism - Giotto, Masaccio, Donatello, Botticelli, Leonardo da Vinci ('Mona Lisa', 'The Last Supper'), Michelangelo (the Sistine Chapel ceiling, 'David'), Raphael ('The School of Athens'), and Titian. Northern Renaissance artists included Jan van Eyck, Albrecht Dürer and Pieter Bruegel. Literature included Machiavelli's 'The Prince' (1513), Castiglione's 'The Courtier', Erasmus's 'In Praise of Folly', Thomas More's 'Utopia', Cervantes's 'Don Quixote' and Shakespeare. Science advanced with Copernicus (heliocentric theory, 1543), Vesalius (anatomy) and later Galileo.
Humanism emphasised classical texts and human intellectual capacities and became a major feature of Renaissance scholarship.

Renaissance humanism was a programme of education and scholarship based on the studia humanitatis - grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history and moral philosophy - studied through classical Latin and Greek texts. Humanists searched monasteries for lost manuscripts, edited texts critically and wrote elegant Latin. They believed education should produce virtuous, eloquent citizens capable of active public life ('civic humanism' of Leonardo Bruni in Florence).

Pico della Mirandola's 'Oration on the Dignity of Man' (1486) celebrated human freedom and potential. Marsilio Ficino translated Plato for the Platonic Academy of Florence. Lorenzo Valla exposed the forged 'Donation of Constantine' through textual criticism. Northern 'Christian humanists' such as Erasmus (who published a Greek New Testament, 1516) and Thomas More applied humanist scholarship to reform the Church and society. The printing press (Gutenberg, c. 1450) spread humanist works rapidly.
Martin Luther's challenge to the Church contributed to the Protestant Reformation and deep religious division in Europe.

Martin Luther (1483-1546), a German monk and theology professor at Wittenberg, objected to the sale of indulgences (remission of punishment for sins), promoted by Johann Tetzel to finance the rebuilding of St Peter's Basilica. On 31 October 1517 he posted his Ninety-Five Theses.
