Language and tribe: most languages of the region are Tibeto-Burman (Bodo-Garo, Kuki-Chin, Naga, Tani, Meitei), alongside Austroasiatic (Khasi), Indo-Aryan (Assamese, Bengali) and Tai. The category 'tribe', created in colonial ethnography and used in the Constitution, needs critical examination, as it has homogenising and stigmatising aspects but also provides a basis for rights and identity. These issues show how territory, identity, language and constitutional arrangements remain central to Northeast India.
Napoleon rose during the aftermath of the French Revolution, established authoritarian rule and built a European empire before military defeat and exile.

Napoleon Bonaparte (1769-1821), born in Corsica, rose as a brilliant artillery officer in the Revolutionary wars (Toulon, 1793; Italian campaign, 1796-1797; Egyptian expedition, 1798). He seized power in the coup of 18 Brumaire (November 1799), became First Consul, Consul for life (1802) and Emperor (1804). His reforms included the Napoleonic Code (Civil Code, 1804), which established equality before the law, property rights and secular authority; the Concordat with the Pope (1801); the Bank of France; centralised administration through prefects; and the lycées (secondary schools).

He won great victories (Austerlitz, 1805; Jena, 1806; Wagram, 1809), dissolved the Holy Roman Empire (1806) and dominated Europe, but lost the naval battle of Trafalgar (1805) to Nelson. His Continental System (1806) tried to blockade Britain economically. The Peninsular War in Spain (1808-1814) and the disastrous invasion of Russia (1812), where the 'Grand Army' of 600,000 was destroyed, led to his defeat at Leipzig (Battle of the Nations, 1813) and exile to Elba (1814). He returned for the 'Hundred Days' but was defeated at Waterloo (18 June 1815) by Wellington and Blücher and exiled to St Helena, where he died in 1821. He spread revolutionary ideas such as legal equality and nationalism across Europe.
The Congress of Vienna reorganised Europe after Napoleon and attempted to restore political stability and a balance of power.

The Congress of Vienna (September 1814 - June 1815) was attended by the great powers: Austria (represented by Prince Klemens von Metternich, the dominant figure), Russia (Tsar Alexander I), Prussia (Hardenberg), Britain (Castlereagh) and France (Talleyrand). Its principles were legitimacy (restoring the old ruling dynasties, such as the Bourbons in France, Spain and Naples), the balance of power, compensation for the victors and containment of France.

Territorial changes: the Netherlands and Belgium were united as a buffer against France; Prussia gained the Rhineland and part of Saxony; Austria gained Lombardy and Venetia; Russia gained most of Poland (Congress Poland); Britain gained colonies (Cape Colony, Ceylon, Malta); the German Confederation of 39 states was created; Norway went to Sweden; and Switzerland's neutrality was recognised. The 'Concert of Europe' (Quadruple Alliance, later Quintuple) and the Holy Alliance maintained the settlement through congresses. It kept general peace in Europe until 1914, but it ignored nationalism and liberalism, leading to revolutions in 1820, 1830 and 1848.
Italian unification brought separate states into a single kingdom through nationalism, diplomacy, war and popular action.

After 1815, Italy was divided into several states: the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia, the Austrian-controlled Lombardy and Venetia, the Papal States, the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies (Naples and Sicily), and the duchies of Parma, Modena and Tuscany. The Risorgimento (resurgence) involved secret societies (the Carbonari), Giuseppe Mazzini's 'Young Italy' (1831) promoting a republic, and the revolutions of 1848, which failed.

Count Camillo di Cavour, Prime Minister of Piedmont under King Victor Emmanuel II, modernised Piedmont and used diplomacy: Piedmont joined the Crimean War (1855) and allied with Napoleon III of France, defeating Austria (1859; battles of Magenta and Solferino) to gain Lombardy; the central Italian states joined through plebiscites (1860). Giuseppe Garibaldi with his 'Thousand Red Shirts' conquered Sicily and Naples (1860) and handed them to Victor Emmanuel, who became King of Italy in 1861. Venetia was gained in 1866 (after Prussia defeated Austria) and Rome in 1870 (after French troops withdrew during the Franco-Prussian War), becoming the capital in 1871.
German unification was achieved under Prussian leadership and transformed the European balance of power.

After 1815, Germany consisted of 39 states in the German Confederation, dominated by Austria. The Zollverein (customs union, 1834) under Prussia promoted economic unity. The Frankfurt Parliament of 1848-1849 offered the crown of a united Germany to the Prussian king, Frederick William IV, who refused it.

Otto von Bismarck, Prussian Minister-President from 1862, unified Germany through 'blood and iron'. He strengthened the army and fought three wars: against Denmark (1864) over Schleswig and Holstein; against Austria (Seven Weeks' War, 1866, battle of Sadowa/Königgrätz), which excluded Austria from German affairs and created the North German Confederation; and against France (Franco-Prussian War, 1870-1871), provoked by the Ems Telegram, in which France was defeated at Sedan and lost Alsace-Lorraine. The German Empire was proclaimed at the Hall of Mirrors in Versailles on 18 January 1871, with William I as Kaiser and Bismarck as Chancellor. A united Germany became the strongest power in continental Europe.
The Industrial Revolution introduced mechanised production, factories and major changes in transport, labour and social organisation.

The Industrial Revolution began in Britain from about 1760 because of its coal and iron resources, capital from trade and colonies, agricultural revolution (enclosures, crop rotation) which released labour, a large domestic and colonial market, political stability, and inventions. Key inventions: in textiles - John Kay's flying shuttle (1733), James Hargreaves' spinning jenny (1764), Richard Arkwright's water frame (1769), Samuel Crompton's mule (1779), Edmund Cartwright's power loom (1785) and Eli Whitney's cotton gin (1793); in power - James Watt's improved steam engine (1769); in iron - Abraham Darby's coke smelting and Henry Cort's puddling process; and in transport - canals, George Stephenson's locomotive 'Rocket' (1829) and railways (Liverpool-Manchester, 1830) and steamships.

It spread to Belgium, France, Germany, the USA and Japan in the nineteenth century; a 'Second Industrial Revolution' (from about 1870) introduced steel, electricity, chemicals and oil. Effects: factory system, urbanisation, a working class living in poor conditions (child labour, long hours), the rise of capitalism and the middle class, trade unions, socialist ideas (Marx and Engels' 'Communist Manifesto', 1848), factory laws, imperialism to secure raw materials and markets, and environmental pollution.
Industrial and commercial growth strengthened new middle-class groups associated with business, professions and urban society.

The middle class (bourgeoisie) included industrialists, merchants, bankers, professionals (lawyers, doctors, engineers, teachers) and clerks. They grew in number and wealth with industrialisation and commerce, and believed in individual effort, property, education, thrift and respectability. They supported liberalism - constitutional government, freedom of the press and speech, free trade (Adam Smith's 'The Wealth of Nations', 1776) and limited government.

In Britain, middle-class pressure led to the Reform Act of 1832, which extended voting rights to middle-class men, and the repeal of the Corn Laws (1846). In France, they led the revolutions of 1830 and 1848; in Germany, they supported national unification. They also promoted social reforms, education and the ideal of a domestic family life ('Victorian values'). Marxists saw the bourgeoisie as the ruling class of capitalism opposed to the proletariat.
European powers expanded political and economic control over large parts of Asia during the age of imperialism.

Britain consolidated its rule in India (Crown rule from 1858), conquered Burma (1885), Malaya and Singapore, and fought the Opium Wars (1839-1842, 1856-1860) with China, gaining Hong Kong and opening treaty ports. France conquered Indochina (Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos) from 1858 to 1893. The Dutch extended control over Indonesia. Russia expanded into Central Asia and the Far East. The USA took the Philippines (1898). Japan, after the Meiji Restoration (1868), became an imperialist power, defeating China (1894-1895, gaining Taiwan) and Russia (1904-1905), and annexing Korea (1910).

China was divided into 'spheres of influence' by European powers and Japan; the USA proposed the 'Open Door Policy' (1899). Only Japan and Siam (Thailand) avoided colonisation. Motives for imperialism included economic interests (markets, raw materials, investment - J. A. Hobson and Lenin's 'Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism', 1916), strategic rivalry, nationalism, Social Darwinism and the 'civilising mission' ('the white man's burden', Rudyard Kipling).
European powers rapidly partitioned much of Africa in the late nineteenth century.

In 1870, Europeans controlled only about 10 percent of Africa, mostly coastal areas; by 1914, they controlled about 90 percent. The Berlin Conference (1884-1885), called by Bismarck, laid down rules for partition: a European power had to effectively occupy territory to claim it. King Leopold II of Belgium got the Congo Free State as his personal property, where terrible atrocities were committed in the rubber trade.

Britain ('Cape to Cairo', Cecil Rhodes) took Egypt (1882), Sudan, Nigeria, the Gold Coast, Kenya, Uganda, Rhodesia and South Africa (after the Boer War, 1899-1902); France took most of West and North Africa (Algeria, Tunisia, Morocco, Senegal, French Sudan) and Madagascar; Germany took Togo, Cameroon, South-West Africa (Namibia, where the Herero and Nama genocide took place, 1904-1908) and Tanganyika; Italy took Libya, Eritrea and Somalia; Portugal kept Angola and Mozambique. Only Ethiopia (which defeated Italy at Adwa, 1896) and Liberia remained independent. Resistance included the Ashanti, Zulu (Isandlwana, 1879), Maji Maji (1905-1907) and Mahdist Sudan. Artificial borders drawn in Europe caused later conflicts.
The Monroe Doctrine declared opposition to new European colonial intervention in the Americas and became important in US foreign policy.

US President James Monroe announced the doctrine in his message to Congress on 2 December 1823, largely written by Secretary of State John Quincy Adams. It declared that the Americas were no longer open to European colonisation; that any European intervention in the independent states of the Western Hemisphere would be considered a threat to the USA; and that the USA would not interfere in European affairs or existing European colonies.

It was a response to fears that European powers (the Holy Alliance) would help Spain recover its Latin American colonies, which had become independent (1810-1825), and to Russian claims on the Pacific coast. Britain, interested in Latin American trade, supported it with its navy. The Roosevelt Corollary (1904) of Theodore Roosevelt claimed a US right to intervene in Latin American countries to maintain order ('big stick' policy). The doctrine became the basis of US dominance in the Western Hemisphere.
The war marked a major expansion of United States influence overseas.

Causes: the Cuban struggle for independence from Spain (1895), Spanish brutality (General Weyler's reconcentration camps), sensational 'yellow journalism' by newspapers of William Randolph Hearst and Joseph Pulitzer, American economic interests in Cuban sugar and the mysterious explosion of the battleship USS Maine in Havana harbour (February 1898), which killed 266 sailors ('Remember the Maine!').

The war (April-August 1898) was short: Commodore George Dewey destroyed the Spanish fleet at Manila Bay; Theodore Roosevelt's 'Rough Riders' fought at San Juan Hill in Cuba. By the Treaty of Paris (December 1898), Spain gave Cuba independence (under US influence - the Platt Amendment, 1901, allowed US intervention and the base at Guantanamo Bay), and ceded Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines to the USA for 20 million dollars. Hawaii was annexed separately (1898). The Philippine-American War (1899-1902) followed. The war made the USA a world power with overseas colonies.
Militarism, alliances, imperial rivalry, nationalism and the Balkan crisis contributed to the outbreak of war in 1914.

Long-term causes (often remembered as MAIN): Militarism - an arms race, especially the Anglo-German naval race (Dreadnought battleships) and military plans like Germany's Schlieffen Plan; Alliances - the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy, 1882) and the Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain, formed by the Franco-Russian Alliance 1894, Entente Cordiale 1904 and Anglo-Russian Entente 1907); Imperialism - colonial rivalries, the Moroccan crises (1905, 1911); and Nationalism - French desire for revenge over Alsace-Lorraine, Pan-Slavism, Serbian nationalism and German ambitions (Weltpolitik under Kaiser William II).

The Balkans were the 'powder keg of Europe': Austria-Hungary's annexation of Bosnia (1908) angered Serbia; the Balkan Wars (1912-1913) increased tensions. The immediate cause was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb of the Black Hand society. Austria-Hungary, backed by Germany's 'blank cheque', issued an ultimatum to Serbia and declared war on 28 July 1914; Russia mobilised; Germany declared war on Russia and France and invaded Belgium, bringing Britain in (4 August 1914). The Fischer thesis (1961) emphasised Germany's responsibility.

sections.title: Peace Settlement and League of Nations

blocks.text: The postwar settlement reshaped Europe, while the League of Nations was created to promote collective security but had serious weaknesses.

The Paris Peace Conference (1919) was dominated by the 'Big Four': Woodrow Wilson (USA), David Lloyd George (Britain), Georges Clemenceau (France) and Vittorio Orlando (Italy). Wilson's Fourteen Points (January 1918) called for open diplomacy, free trade, disarmament, self-determination and a League of Nations. The Treaty of Versailles (28 June 1919) with Germany included the 'war guilt' clause (Article 231), heavy reparations (fixed at 132 billion gold marks in 1921), loss of Alsace-Lorraine to France, the Polish Corridor, the Saar under League control, loss of all colonies, demilitarisation of the Rhineland and limits on the army (100,000 men) and navy. Other treaties: St Germain (Austria), Trianon (Hungary), Neuilly (Bulgaria) and Sèvres (Turkey, revised at Lausanne, 1923). New states emerged: Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, the Baltic states.

The League of Nations (founded 1920, headquarters Geneva) aimed at collective security, disarmament and settling disputes. It had an Assembly, Council, Secretariat, the Permanent Court of International Justice and agencies such as the International Labour Organization (ILO). It settled some minor disputes (the Aaland Islands, 1921) and did valuable humanitarian work. Weaknesses: the USA never joined (the Senate rejected the treaty); Germany and the USSR were excluded at first; decisions required unanimity; it had no army; and Britain and France were reluctant. It failed to stop Japan in Manchuria (1931), Italy in Ethiopia (1935-1936) and German aggression, and collapsed with the Second World War. It was replaced by the UN in 1945-1946.
The February and October Revolutions ended Tsarist rule and brought the Bolsheviks to power.

Causes: Tsarist autocracy under Nicholas II; poverty of peasants (serfdom was abolished only in 1861) and workers; the defeat by Japan (1904-1905) and the 1905 Revolution (Bloody Sunday), which led to the Duma (parliament) with limited powers; the influence of Rasputin at court; and especially the heavy losses, food shortages and economic collapse caused by the First World War. Marxist parties included the Social Democrats, split into Bolsheviks (Lenin) and Mensheviks (1903).

The February Revolution (March 1917, Western calendar): strikes and bread riots in Petrograd, joined by soldiers, forced Nicholas II to abdicate. A Provisional Government (Prince Lvov, then Alexander Kerensky) shared power with the Petrograd Soviet ('dual power'), but continued the war. Lenin returned (April Theses: 'Peace, Land, Bread' and 'All power to the Soviets'). In the October Revolution (7 November 1917), the Bolsheviks, led by Lenin and Trotsky, seized power. They withdrew from the war (Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, March 1918), nationalised land and industry, and won the Civil War (1918-1921) against the 'Whites' and foreign intervention. The USSR was formed in 1922. Lenin's New Economic Policy (1921) allowed some private trade; after his death (1924), Stalin introduced Five-Year Plans and collectivisation.
Fascism promoted authoritarian nationalism and rejected liberal democracy. It became especially associated with Mussolini's Italy.

Benito Mussolini, a former socialist, founded the Fascist movement (Fasci di Combattimento) in 1919. Italy was discontented after the war ('mutilated victory' - it did not gain the territories it expected), and suffered unemployment, inflation, strikes and fear of communism. Fascist squads (Blackshirts) attacked socialists. After the 'March on Rome' (October 1922), King Victor Emmanuel III appointed Mussolini Prime Minister. After the murder of the socialist Giacomo Matteotti (1924), Mussolini established a dictatorship (1925-1926), calling himself Il Duce.

Features of fascism: extreme nationalism; a one-party totalitarian state ('Everything within the state, nothing outside the state'); the cult of the leader; rejection of liberal democracy, socialism and class struggle; the corporate state (organising employers and workers in corporations under state control); glorification of war and violence; propaganda and youth organisations. Mussolini signed the Lateran Treaty (1929) with the Pope, invaded Ethiopia (1935-1936), formed the Rome-Berlin Axis (1936) and joined the Second World War. He was overthrown in 1943 and killed by partisans in 1945.
Nazism combined dictatorship, extreme nationalism, racism and antisemitism under Adolf Hitler.

Adolf Hitler, an Austrian-born veteran, led the National Socialist German Workers' Party (NSDAP). After the failed Munich Beer Hall Putsch (1923), he wrote 'Mein Kampf' in prison, setting out his ideas: the superiority of the 'Aryan' race, antisemitism, Lebensraum (living space) in the East, hatred of communism and the Treaty of Versailles. Germany's Weimar Republic (1919-1933) faced reparations, hyperinflation (1923), political violence and especially the Great Depression, which caused mass unemployment (6 million by 1932). The Nazis became the largest party in the Reichstag (July 1932), and Hitler was appointed Chancellor on 30 January 1933.

After the Reichstag fire (February 1933), the Enabling Act (March 1933) gave him dictatorial powers. He banned other parties and trade unions, purged rivals (the Night of the Long Knives, 1934), became Führer after Hindenburg's death (1934), and used the Gestapo, SS and propaganda (Goebbels). Jews were persecuted - the Nuremberg Laws (1935) removed their citizenship; Kristallnacht (November 1938); and in the Second World War, the Holocaust killed about six million Jews, along with Roma, disabled people and others, in concentration and extermination camps such as Auschwitz. Hitler rearmed Germany, remilitarised the Rhineland (1936), annexed Austria (Anschluss, 1938) and the Sudetenland (Munich Agreement, 1938), and invaded Poland (1939).
The worldwide economic crisis beginning in 1929 produced unemployment, social distress and political instability.

The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 ('Black Tuesday', 29 October) in New York began the Great Depression. Causes included overproduction in agriculture and industry, unequal distribution of income, speculation and buying shares on credit, weak banks, high tariffs (the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, 1930) and the dependence of Europe on American loans (the Dawes and Young Plans).

Effects: banks failed, industrial production fell by nearly half in the USA, world trade fell by about two-thirds, and unemployment reached 25 percent in the USA and 30 percent in Germany. In India, prices of agricultural products fell sharply, hurting peasants and contributing to the Civil Disobedience movement. Responses: Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal (1933), with public works, social security and bank regulation; John Maynard Keynes' theory of government spending; protectionism; and in some countries, the rise of dictatorships (Hitler) and militarism (Japan). The Depression discredited liberal capitalism for many and contributed to the Second World War.
Expansionist dictatorships, unresolved tensions and failures of collective security contributed to war in 1939. The conflict transformed global politics.

Causes: the harsh Treaty of Versailles and German resentment; the failure of the League of Nations; the Great Depression; the rise of fascism and Nazism; Japanese militarism (invasion of Manchuria, 1931; war with China from 1937); the policy of appeasement by Britain (Neville Chamberlain) and France (the Munich Agreement, 1938); the Rome-Berlin-Tokyo Axis; and the Nazi-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact (August 1939). Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939; Britain and France declared war on 3 September.

Course: German Blitzkrieg conquered Poland, Denmark, Norway, the Netherlands, Belgium and France (1940); Britain survived the Battle of Britain (1940); Germany invaded the USSR (Operation Barbarossa, June 1941); Japan attacked Pearl Harbor (7 December 1941), bringing the USA into the war. Turning points: Midway (1942), El Alamein (1942) and Stalingrad (1942-1943). The Allies landed in Normandy (D-Day, 6 June 1944). Germany surrendered on 8 May 1945 (VE Day) after Hitler's suicide. After atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Japan surrendered (15 August, formally 2 September 1945). About 70-85 million people died. Results: the defeat of fascism, the rise of the USA and USSR as superpowers, the Cold War, the division of Germany, decolonisation and the founding of the UN.

sections.title: Race to Build the Atomic Bomb

blocks.text: During the Second World War, the United States led the Manhattan Project to develop atomic weapons.

In 1938, German scientists Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann discovered nuclear fission; Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained it. Fearing that Nazi Germany would build an atomic bomb, physicists Leo Szilard and Albert Einstein wrote a letter to President Roosevelt (August 1939). The Manhattan Project (1942-1946), led by General Leslie Groves with J. Robert Oppenheimer as scientific director at Los Alamos, New Mexico, employed over 100,000 people, with British and Canadian participation.

The first atomic bomb test, 'Trinity', took place on 16 July 1945 in New Mexico. The USA dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima ('Little Boy', uranium, 6 August 1945) and Nagasaki ('Fat Man', plutonium, 9 August 1945), killing about 200,000 people by the end of 1945, many from radiation. Historians debate whether the bombing was necessary to end the war, or partly intended to intimidate the USSR. The USSR tested its first bomb in 1949, beginning the nuclear arms race of the Cold War.
The United Nations was established in 1945 to promote international peace, security and cooperation.

The Atlantic Charter (1941) of Roosevelt and Churchill and the Declaration by United Nations (1942) prepared the way. The Dumbarton Oaks Conference (1944) drafted proposals; the Yalta Conference (1945) agreed on voting arrangements; and the UN Charter was signed by 50 countries at the San Francisco Conference on 26 June 1945. The UN came into existence on 24 October 1945 (UN Day), with its headquarters in New York. India was a founding member.

Main organs: the General Assembly (all members, one vote each); the Security Council (five permanent members with veto power - the USA, USSR/Russia, Britain, France and China - and ten non-permanent members), responsible for international peace and security; the Economic and Social Council; the Trusteeship Council (now inactive); the International Court of Justice (The Hague); and the Secretariat headed by the Secretary-General. Specialised agencies include UNESCO, WHO, FAO, UNICEF, ILO, IMF and the World Bank. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) was adopted. The UN has conducted peacekeeping missions (India has been a major contributor), supported decolonisation and development, but has been criticised for the veto and Cold War paralysis.

Napoleon rose from the revolutionary era and dominated much of Europe before his defeat. The Congress of Vienna then sought to restore stability and prevent domination by a single power.

Nationalism remained a powerful force. Italy unified through the efforts of political leaders, nationalists and military campaigns, while Germany unified under Prussian leadership.

These changes transformed the political map and balance of power in nineteenth-century Europe.

Napoleon: rose through Revolutionary wars; became First Consul (1799) and Emperor (1804); introduced the Civil Code, Concordat, centralised administration and education; conquered much of Europe (Austerlitz, Jena, Wagram), reorganised Germany and Italy and spread revolutionary principles; failed with the Continental System, Spain and Russia (1812); defeated at Leipzig (1813) and Waterloo (1815). Congress of Vienna (1814-1815): Metternich, Castlereagh, Alexander I, Hardenberg and Talleyrand restored legitimate monarchs, created a balance of power and buffer states, and established the Concert of Europe. It brought peace among great powers but suppressed liberalism and nationalism, leading to revolutions in 1820-1821, 1830 and 1848.

Italian unification: the Risorgimento - Mazzini (the soul, Young Italy), Cavour (the brain, diplomacy and alliance with France), Garibaldi (the sword, the Thousand) and Victor Emmanuel II; wars of 1859 and 1866; Kingdom of Italy proclaimed 1861; Rome captured 1870. German unification: the Zollverein, the failure of 1848, Bismarck's 'blood and iron', three wars (Denmark 1864, Austria 1866, France 1870-1871) and the proclamation of the German Empire at Versailles (1871).

Effects: the emergence of two new great powers changed the balance of power; Germany became the dominant continental power, leading to French hostility over Alsace-Lorraine and the formation of alliances that contributed to the First World War. Nationalism, initially liberal, increasingly became conservative and aggressive in the late nineteenth century.

The Industrial Revolution began a major transformation in production, transport, urbanisation and class relations. Industrial and commercial expansion strengthened the middle classes.

Industrial powers sought markets, raw materials and strategic advantage abroad. Imperialism expanded in Asia, while the Scramble for Africa produced rapid European partition.

In the Americas, the Monroe Doctrine and Spanish-American War illustrate the growing international role of the United States.

Industrial Revolution: began in Britain (c. 1760) due to coal, iron, capital, colonies, agricultural changes and inventions (textile machines, steam engine, railways); spread to Europe, the USA and Japan; a Second Industrial Revolution (steel, electricity, chemicals, oil, automobiles) followed. Social effects: urbanisation, factory labour, poor working and living conditions, child labour, the rise of the working class and trade unions, socialism (Marx), and reforms (Factory Acts, extension of the vote). The middle classes grew powerful, promoting liberalism, free trade, education and parliamentary reform (Reform Act 1832).

Imperialism: motivated by the need for raw materials, markets and investment (Hobson, Lenin), strategic rivalry, nationalism, missionary zeal and Social Darwinism. In Asia: British India and Burma, French Indochina, Dutch Indonesia, the Opium Wars and spheres of influence in China, Japanese imperialism (Taiwan, Korea) and the US annexation of the Philippines. In Africa: the Scramble for Africa after the Berlin Conference (1884-1885), leaving only Ethiopia and Liberia independent, with brutal exploitation (the Congo) and resistance movements.

Americas: the Monroe Doctrine (1823) opposed new European colonisation, and the Roosevelt Corollary (1904) asserted US police power. The Spanish-American War (1898) made the USA a colonial power (Puerto Rico, Guam, the Philippines, influence over Cuba). Imperialism led to rivalries that contributed to the First World War and later to anti-colonial nationalism.

sections.title: First World War and Interwar Turmoil

blocks.text:
The First World War resulted from a combination of alliances, militarism, imperial rivalry, nationalism and immediate crisis. Its enormous destruction produced a new peace settlement and the League of Nations.

The Russian Revolutions of 1917 transformed Russia and established a communist state. In the interwar period, Fascism and Nazism grew amid political and social crisis.

The Great Depression further weakened economies and democratic institutions in many countries.

First World War (1914-1918): long-term causes - militarism, alliances, imperialism, nationalism (MAIN) and the Balkan crisis; immediate cause - the Sarajevo assassination (28 June 1914). Course: the Western Front (trench warfare - the Marne, Verdun, the Somme), the Eastern Front, Gallipoli, the war at sea (U-boats, the sinking of the Lusitania), US entry (1917) and the Armistice (11 November 1918). About 9-10 million soldiers died. New weapons included machine guns, poison gas, tanks and aircraft.

Peace and League: the Paris Peace Conference and the Treaty of Versailles (war guilt, reparations, territorial losses, disarmament) created resentment in Germany; new states emerged on the principle of self-determination; the League of Nations was created but was weak (no US, unanimity, no army) and failed in Manchuria and Ethiopia. Russian Revolutions (1917): the February Revolution ended Tsarism; the October Revolution brought the Bolsheviks to power under Lenin; the Civil War, War Communism, NEP and Stalin's Five-Year Plans and collectivisation followed, creating the world's first communist state.

Interwar turmoil: fascism in Italy (Mussolini, 1922) and Nazism in Germany (Hitler, 1933) arose from postwar discontent, economic crisis, fear of communism and weak democracies. The Great Depression (from 1929) caused mass unemployment and political extremism; responses included the New Deal and Keynesian ideas. Militarist Japan, aggressive Italy and Germany, and the policy of appeasement set the stage for the Second World War.

sections.title: Second World War and the United Nations

blocks.text:
The Second World War emerged from expansionist policies, unresolved post-1918 tensions and the failure to contain aggression. It became a global conflict with unprecedented destruction.

Scientific and military competition included the race to build the atomic bomb. Atomic weapons were used against Japan in 1945.

The United Nations was established in the same year to create a new framework for international cooperation and collective security.

Causes: the Treaty of Versailles, the failure of the League, the Great Depression, fascist and Nazi expansionism, Japanese militarism, appeasement (Munich, 1938) and the Nazi-Soviet Pact (1939). The war began with Germany's invasion of Poland (1 September 1939). Phases: Axis victories (1939-1942) in Europe, North Africa and Asia; turning points (Midway, El Alamein, Stalingrad, 1942-1943); and Allied victories (1943-1945), including the D-Day landings (1944), the Soviet advance to Berlin and the Pacific island-hopping campaign. The Holocaust killed six million Jews.

The atomic bomb: nuclear fission (1938), the Einstein-Szilard letter (1939), the Manhattan Project (Oppenheimer, Los Alamos), the Trinity test (July 1945) and the bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki (August 1945), leading to Japan's surrender. Consequences: the USA and USSR emerged as superpowers; Europe was devastated and divided; Germany and Korea were divided; colonial empires were weakened, leading to decolonisation (including India's independence in 1947); the nuclear age and arms race began; the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials prosecuted war crimes.

The United Nations (1945): established by the San Francisco Charter to maintain peace, promote cooperation and human rights; its organs include the General Assembly, the Security Council (with veto powers of five permanent members), ECOSOC, the International Court of Justice and the Secretariat, along with specialised agencies. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) set global standards. Compared with the League, the UN has wider membership and peacekeeping forces, though the veto has often paralysed it.
The postwar rivalry between the United States and Soviet Union divided Europe and created competing political and military blocs.

Origins: ideological conflict between capitalism and communism, wartime disagreements (the Yalta and Potsdam conferences, 1945), Soviet control of Eastern Europe (Churchill's 'Iron Curtain' speech at Fulton, 1946), and the US policy of containment (George Kennan). The Truman Doctrine (1947) offered support to countries resisting communism (Greece and Turkey); the Marshall Plan (1947-1951) provided about 13 billion dollars to rebuild Western Europe; the USSR responded with Cominform (1947) and Comecon (1949).

The Berlin Blockade (1948-1949) and Berlin Airlift; the division of Germany into the Federal Republic (West) and the German Democratic Republic (East) in 1949; NATO (1949) and the Warsaw Pact (1955); the Soviet atomic bomb (1949); the Korean War (1950-1953); the Hungarian uprising crushed by the USSR (1956); the arms and space race (Sputnik, 1957); and the construction of the Berlin Wall (August 1961). Khrushchev proposed 'peaceful coexistence' after Stalin's death (1953), but tensions continued.
The 1962 confrontation over Soviet missiles in Cuba brought the superpowers close to nuclear war.

After Fidel Castro's revolution in Cuba (1959) and the failed US-backed Bay of Pigs invasion (April 1961), Khrushchev secretly placed nuclear missiles in Cuba, partly to protect Cuba and to balance US missiles in Turkey and Italy. On 14 October 1962, US U-2 spy planes photographed the missile sites. President John F. Kennedy announced a naval 'quarantine' (blockade) of Cuba on 22 October.

For thirteen days the world was close to nuclear war. On 28 October, Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles in exchange for a US promise not to invade Cuba, and secretly the USA agreed to remove its Jupiter missiles from Turkey. Results: a Moscow-Washington 'hotline' (1963), the Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963), and a realisation of the dangers of nuclear confrontation, contributing to détente.
Détente refers to the easing of Cold War tensions during parts of the 1960s and 1970s before renewed confrontation.

Détente (French for 'relaxation') refers to the easing of tensions from the late 1960s to the late 1970s, under US President Richard Nixon and National Security Adviser Henry Kissinger and Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev. Factors: the dangers shown by the Cuban crisis, the cost of the arms race, the Sino-Soviet split, the US involvement in Vietnam, and West German Chancellor Willy Brandt's Ostpolitik (normalising relations with Eastern Europe).

Achievements: the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (1968); Nixon's visit to China (1972); the Strategic Arms Limitation Treaty (SALT I) and the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty (1972); the Apollo-Soyuz joint space mission (1975); and the Helsinki Accords (1975), which recognised Europe's borders and committed signatories to human rights. Détente ended with the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (December 1979), the US boycott of the Moscow Olympics (1980) and Ronald Reagan's arms build-up ('Second Cold War'), until Gorbachev's reforms led to the end of the Cold War (1989-1991).
Western and Eastern Europe rebuilt after the Second World War, though under different economic and political systems.

Western Europe: the Marshall Plan, the Bretton Woods system (IMF and World Bank, 1944), Keynesian economic policies, the welfare state (Britain's National Health Service, 1948) and European integration - the European Coal and Steel Community (1951) and the European Economic Community (Treaty of Rome, 1957) - led to rapid growth in the 1950s and 1960s, called the 'economic miracle' (Wirtschaftswunder) in West Germany, the 'Trente Glorieuses' in France and the 'economic boom' in Italy.

Eastern Europe: under Soviet control, countries adopted Soviet-style planned economies, collectivised agriculture and nationalised industry, coordinated through Comecon. They achieved industrial growth and full employment, but with lower living standards, shortages of consumer goods and political repression, leading to uprisings in East Germany (1953), Hungary (1956), Czechoslovakia (the Prague Spring, 1968) and Poland (Solidarity, 1980-1981). The contrast between East and West contributed to the eventual collapse of communism in 1989.
European empires weakened after 1945 and nationalist movements created independent states across Asia and Africa.

Factors: the weakening of European powers in the Second World War; the growth of nationalist movements; the Atlantic Charter's principle of self-determination; the opposition of the USA and USSR to colonialism; and the UN. Asia: India and Pakistan (1947), Burma and Ceylon (1948), Indonesia (1949, after war with the Dutch), Indochina (after the French defeat at Dien Bien Phu, 1954), Malaya (1957). Africa: Ghana under Kwame Nkrumah (1957) was the first sub-Saharan country to become independent; 1960 was the 'Year of Africa', with 17 countries gaining independence; Algeria won independence after a brutal war with France (1954-1962); Kenya after the Mau Mau uprising (1963); Portuguese colonies after the 1974 revolution in Portugal; Zimbabwe (1980) and Namibia (1990).

Decolonisation was peaceful in some cases and violent in others. New nations faced problems of poverty, artificial borders, ethnic conflict, military coups and neo-colonialism (continued economic dependence on former colonial powers). The UN's Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples (1960) supported the process.
The Chinese Communist victory in 1949 created the People's Republic of China and transformed Asian politics.

After the 1911 Revolution, China was divided among warlords. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP, founded 1921) and the Kuomintang (KMT) cooperated in the First United Front (1923-1927), but Chiang Kai-shek turned on the communists in the Shanghai massacre (1927). The communists, led by Mao Zedong, built rural bases (the Jiangxi Soviet), and escaped encirclement through the Long March (1934-1935) to Yan'an. During the war with Japan (1937-1945), the Second United Front formed, and the communists expanded their support among peasants through guerrilla warfare and land reform.

In the civil war (1946-1949), the communists defeated the KMT, which was weakened by corruption, inflation and loss of popular support. Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China on 1 October 1949 at Tiananmen Square in Beijing; Chiang fled to Taiwan. The revolution created the world's most populous communist state, signed the Sino-Soviet Treaty (1950) and changed the balance of power in Asia, leading to US involvement in Korea and support for Taiwan.
The Korean War became a major Cold War conflict and left Korea divided.

Korea, a Japanese colony since 1910, was divided at the 38th parallel in 1945, with Soviet troops in the north and US troops in the south. In 1948, the Republic of Korea (South, under Syngman Rhee) and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North, under Kim Il-sung) were established. On 25 June 1950, North Korea invaded the South with Soviet and Chinese approval.

The UN Security Council (with the USSR absent in protest over China's seat) authorised a UN force, mostly American, under General Douglas MacArthur. After the Inchon landing (September 1950), UN forces pushed north towards the Yalu River, provoking Chinese intervention with hundreds of thousands of 'volunteers' (October 1950). The war became a stalemate near the 38th parallel. MacArthur was dismissed by Truman (1951) for wanting to attack China. An armistice was signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953; no peace treaty has been signed, and Korea remains divided by the Demilitarised Zone. About 3 million people died. India played a role through the Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission chaired by General K. S. Thimayya.
Vietnam's wars involved anti-colonial struggle, civil conflict and Cold War intervention.

First Indochina War (1946-1954): Ho Chi Minh's Viet Minh declared Vietnam's independence (September 1945) and fought France. The French defeat at Dien Bien Phu (May 1954) led to the Geneva Accords (1954), which divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel, with elections planned for 1956 that never took place. North Vietnam was communist; South Vietnam was led by Ngo Dinh Diem with US support.

Second Indochina (Vietnam) War (c. 1955-1975): the communist Viet Cong (National Liberation Front) fought in the South with Northern support. The USA increased involvement based on the 'domino theory'; after the Gulf of Tonkin incident (1964), President Lyndon Johnson sent over 500,000 troops and bombed the North (Operation Rolling Thunder). The Tet Offensive (1968) turned US public opinion against the war; the anti-war movement grew. Nixon's 'Vietnamisation' reduced US troops, and the Paris Peace Accords (1973) ended US involvement. North Vietnamese forces captured Saigon on 30 April 1975, uniting Vietnam. About 2-3 million Vietnamese died. Wars also affected Cambodia (Khmer Rouge genocide, 1975-1979) and Laos.
The Arab-Israeli conflict became one of the major continuing political conflicts of the postwar world.

Background: Zionism (Theodor Herzl, 1896) sought a Jewish homeland in Palestine; the Balfour Declaration (1917) by Britain supported a 'national home for the Jewish people'; Britain ruled Palestine under a League of Nations mandate, and Jewish immigration increased, especially after the Holocaust, causing conflict with Arabs. The UN Partition Plan (1947) proposed separate Jewish and Arab states. Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948; the first Arab-Israeli war followed, and about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled (the Nakba).

Later wars: the Suez Crisis (1956), when Israel, Britain and France attacked Egypt after Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal; the Six-Day War (1967), when Israel captured the West Bank, East Jerusalem, Gaza, the Sinai and the Golan Heights; the Yom Kippur War (1973) and the Arab oil embargo. The Camp David Accords (1978) led to the Egypt-Israel peace treaty (1979). The Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO, 1964, led by Yasser Arafat) and the intifadas (1987, 2000) continued the struggle; the Oslo Accords (1993) created the Palestinian Authority, but a final settlement has not been achieved. The conflict has continued into the 2020s, including the war in Gaza following the attacks of 7 October 2023.
African decolonisation ended most formal European empires, but new states faced problems of development, Cold War intervention and political stability.

Pan-Africanism, promoted by W. E. B. Du Bois, Marcus Garvey, Kwame Nkrumah and the Pan-African Congresses (Manchester, 1945), inspired the independence movements. The Organisation of African Unity (OAU, 1963) was founded at Addis Ababa to promote unity and end colonialism; it became the African Union (2002). New leaders included Nkrumah (Ghana), Jomo Kenyatta (Kenya), Julius Nyerere (Tanzania, 'ujamaa' socialism), Patrice Lumumba (Congo, assassinated 1961), Léopold Senghor (Senegal) and Gamal Abdel Nasser (Egypt).

Challenges: artificial colonial borders and ethnic divisions (the Nigerian Civil War / Biafra, 1967-1970); military coups and one-party states; Cold War interventions (the Congo crisis, Angola, Ethiopia); dependence on exports of raw materials; debt crises and structural adjustment programmes of the 1980s; famines (Ethiopia, 1984-1985); and the Rwandan genocide (1994). Since the 1990s, many African countries have moved towards multiparty democracy and economic growth.
South Africa's apartheid system ended through prolonged internal resistance, international pressure and political negotiation.

Apartheid ('separateness') was a system of institutionalised racial segregation introduced by the National Party government in 1948 under D. F. Malan. Laws included the Population Registration Act (1950), classifying people by race; the Group Areas Act (1950), segregating residential areas; the Bantu Education Act (1953); pass laws restricting black Africans' movement; and the creation of 'Bantustans' (homelands). Opposition came from the African National Congress (ANC, 1912). The Sharpeville massacre (1960), when police killed 69 protesters, led to the banning of the ANC; Nelson Mandela was imprisoned in 1964 (Rivonia Trial) on Robben Island. The Soweto uprising (1976) and Steve Biko's death in custody (1977) intensified resistance.

International pressure included UN sanctions, sports boycotts and economic disinvestment; India was the first country to impose trade sanctions on South Africa (1946). President F. W. de Klerk lifted the ban on the ANC and released Mandela in February 1990. Negotiations led to the first multiracial elections in April 1994, and Mandela became President. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, 1996) investigated human rights abuses. Mandela and de Klerk shared the Nobel Peace Prize (1993).
The Non-Aligned Movement sought political independence from the major Cold War blocs. India became one of its leading members.

The Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) was founded at the Belgrade Conference (1961) by Jawaharlal Nehru (India), Josip Broz Tito (Yugoslavia), Gamal Abdel Nasser (Egypt), Sukarno (Indonesia) and Kwame Nkrumah (Ghana), building on the Bandung Asian-African Conference (1955) and its 'Ten Principles'. It drew on India's Panchsheel principles (1954) of peaceful coexistence, signed with China.

Aims: to stay independent of the US and Soviet blocs; oppose colonialism, racism and apartheid; support disarmament and world peace; and promote economic development and a New International Economic Order (NIEO, 1974). NAM grew to about 120 members, the largest grouping of states after the UN. Critics noted that some members were aligned in practice (India signed a treaty with the USSR in 1971) and that NAM lost relevance after the Cold War, though it continues to meet.
The Group of 77 represented developing countries seeking greater influence and economic justice in the international system.

The Group of 77 (G77) was formed on 15 June 1964 by 77 developing countries at the end of the first United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) in Geneva. Its 'Joint Declaration' called for a fairer world economic system. It now has over 130 members (with China often associated as 'G77 and China') but keeps its original name.

It promotes the collective economic interests of developing countries in the UN, demanding fairer terms of trade, stable prices for primary commodities, access to markets of developed countries, technology transfer, debt relief and development aid. It pushed for the NIEO declaration (1974) and South-South cooperation. In climate negotiations, the G77 and China argue for 'common but differentiated responsibilities'. Its effectiveness has been limited by divisions among its diverse members.
Japan became an economic superpower, while South Korea and Taiwan experienced rapid industrial and economic growth.

Japan: after defeat in 1945, the US occupation under General MacArthur introduced a democratic constitution (1947), which renounced war (Article 9), land reform and the break-up of zaibatsu (business conglomerates). The Korean War boosted Japan's economy. With high savings and investment, government guidance (MITI), lifetime employment, technology adoption and exports (cars, electronics - Toyota, Sony), Japan achieved rapid growth (around 10 percent a year in the 1960s) and became the world's second-largest economy by 1968. The bursting of an asset bubble in 1990-1991 led to the 'lost decade'.

South Korea under Park Chung-hee (1961-1979) and Taiwan under the KMT followed export-oriented industrialisation with strong state guidance, land reform, education and US aid, becoming 'newly industrialised economies' (the 'Four Asian Tigers' with Hong Kong and Singapore). South Korea developed chaebols (Samsung, Hyundai). Both democratised in the late 1980s. Explanations of the 'East Asian miracle' include the developmental state, Confucian values, education, high savings and favourable Cold War conditions.
Relations between communist China and the Soviet Union deteriorated because of ideological and strategic disagreements.

China and the USSR signed the Treaty of Friendship (1950), and the USSR provided aid and technology. Relations deteriorated after Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin (1956) and his policy of 'peaceful coexistence' with the West, which Mao criticised as 'revisionism'. Mao's Great Leap Forward rejected the Soviet development model. The USSR withdrew its technical advisers (1960) and refused to help China build nuclear weapons; China tested its own atomic bomb in 1964.

Other disputes included the Soviet neutrality in the Sino-Indian War (1962), competition for leadership of the communist world and the Third World, and border clashes along the Ussuri River (Zhenbao Island, 1969). The split led China to improve relations with the USA - 'ping-pong diplomacy', Kissinger's secret visit (1971), China's admission to the UN in place of Taiwan (1971) and Nixon's visit (1972). Relations normalised only in 1989 under Gorbachev.
North Korea developed a highly centralised political system combining communist institutions, nationalism and dynastic leadership.

Kim Il-sung (ruled 1948-1994) created a communist state with a personality cult. He developed the ideology of Juche (self-reliance), emphasising independence in politics, economy and defence, and later Songun ('military first' policy, under Kim Jong-il). Power passed dynastically to his son Kim Jong-il (1994-2011) and grandson Kim Jong-un (from 2011), making North Korea a hereditary communist state.

North Korea has a centrally planned economy and is one of the most isolated countries in the world. After the collapse of the USSR, it suffered a severe famine in the 1990s ('the Arduous March'), killing hundreds of thousands. It withdrew from the Non-Proliferation Treaty (2003) and conducted nuclear tests from 2006 and missile tests, leading to UN sanctions. Summits between Kim Jong-un and South Korea's Moon Jae-in and US President Donald Trump (2018-2019) did not produce lasting agreements.
Cold War politics shaped US involvement in Guatemala, Cuba, Chile and Nicaragua amid struggles over inequality, nationalism and socialism.

Guatemala: President Jacobo Árbenz carried out land reform that affected the US-owned United Fruit Company; the CIA organised a coup that overthrew him (1954). Cuba: Fidel Castro and Che Guevara overthrew the dictator Fulgencio Batista (1959); Castro nationalised US property and allied with the USSR; the USA imposed an embargo, sponsored the failed Bay of Pigs invasion (1961) and faced the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962). The 'Alliance for Progress' (1961) of Kennedy offered economic aid to counter revolution.

Chile: the socialist President Salvador Allende, elected in 1970, nationalised copper mines; with US support, General Augusto Pinochet overthrew him in a coup on 11 September 1973, and ruled as dictator until 1990, with widespread human rights abuses and free-market reforms. Nicaragua: the Sandinistas overthrew the Somoza dictatorship (1979); the Reagan administration funded the 'Contra' rebels, leading to the Iran-Contra affair (1986). These cases show how Cold War fears of communism led the USA to support dictatorships and interventions, while Latin American struggles were rooted in inequality, land, foreign economic domination and nationalism.

The Cold War divided the post-1945 world between rival US- and Soviet-led blocs. Europe became an early centre of confrontation. The Cuban Missile Crisis demonstrated the danger of nuclear conflict.

From the 1960s, periods of détente reduced some tensions, although détente later weakened. Meanwhile, Western and Eastern Europe experienced postwar reconstruction and economic recovery under different systems.

Cold War politics therefore combined military rivalry, ideology and economic competition.

Origins and first Cold War (1945-1961): ideological rivalry, the Soviet takeover of Eastern Europe, the Iron Curtain, containment, the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan, the Berlin Blockade and Airlift, NATO (1949) and the Warsaw Pact (1955), the nuclear and space race, the Korean War and the Berlin Wall (1961). Historians debate responsibility: orthodox (Soviet expansionism), revisionist (US economic imperialism) and post-revisionist (mutual misperception) schools.

Crisis and détente: the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) brought the world close to nuclear war and led to the hotline and the Test Ban Treaty (1963). Détente (late 1960s-1970s) included the NPT (1968), SALT I and the ABM Treaty (1972), Ostpolitik and the Helsinki Accords (1975). It collapsed with the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (1979). The Cold War ended after Gorbachev's glasnost and perestroika, the fall of the Berlin Wall (1989), German reunification (1990) and the dissolution of the USSR (December 1991).

Economic recovery: Western Europe recovered quickly with Marshall aid, the welfare state and European integration (ECSC 1951, EEC 1957), achieving an 'economic miracle'; Eastern Europe developed planned economies under Comecon with industrial growth but shortages and repression. Economic competition became part of the Cold War, and the West's economic success contributed to its eventual victory.

sections.title: Decolonisation and Transformation of Asia and Africa

blocks.text:
The end of British rule in India formed part of a wider wave of decolonisation. Southeast Asian nationalism, the Chinese Revolution, the Korean War and the Vietnam Wars reshaped Asia.

The Arab-Israeli conflict became another major source of regional and international tension. In Africa, colonial empires collapsed and pan-Africanism inspired hopes of unity.

New African states nevertheless faced Cold War intervention, poverty, resource conflicts and difficult paths toward democracy. The end of apartheid became a major late-twentieth-century transformation.

Asia: India's independence (1947) inspired others; decolonisation followed in Burma, Ceylon, Indonesia (Sukarno), Malaya, and Indochina. Southeast Asian nationalism included the struggles of Ho Chi Minh, Sukarno and Aung San. The Chinese Revolution (1949) created a communist state; the Korean War (1950-1953) left Korea divided; the Vietnam Wars (1946-1954 and 1955-1975) ended with communist victory and unification. The Arab-Israeli conflict (1948, 1956, 1967, 1973 wars; the Palestinian issue) destabilised West Asia.

Africa: Pan-Africanism and nationalist leaders (Nkrumah, Kenyatta, Nyerere, Lumumba) led to independence for most countries between 1957 and 1975; violent struggles occurred in Algeria, Kenya, Angola, Mozambique and Zimbabwe. The OAU (1963) promoted unity. New states faced artificial borders, ethnic conflict, military coups, one-party rule, Cold War interventions (Congo, Angola), economic dependence, debt and poverty.

End of apartheid: the National Party's apartheid system (from 1948) was resisted by the ANC, Mandela and the black consciousness movement (Biko), with international sanctions. De Klerk's reforms, Mandela's release (1990) and the elections of 1994 ended apartheid, followed by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Decolonisation thus transformed the world from a system of empires into one of nearly 200 sovereign states.

Some states sought greater independence from Cold War blocs. India played an important role in the Non-Aligned Movement, while the Group of 77 pressed economic demands of developing countries.

The idea of a united Third World later became more fragmented because countries had different political systems, interests and development paths.

East Asia also changed rapidly as Japan, South Korea and Taiwan emerged as major economic powers.

Non-alignment: newly independent countries did not want to join either Cold War bloc. Nehru's foreign policy of non-alignment, the Panchsheel principles (1954) and the Bandung Conference (1955) led to the founding of the NAM at Belgrade (1961) by Nehru, Tito, Nasser, Sukarno and Nkrumah. NAM opposed colonialism, racism and apartheid, promoted disarmament and peace, and supported the Third World's economic demands. India played a leading role, though its 1971 treaty with the USSR raised questions about its non-alignment.

G77 and the Third World: the G77 (1964), formed at UNCTAD, demanded a New International Economic Order (1974) with fair trade, commodity price stability, technology transfer and aid. The idea of the 'Third World' (coined by Alfred Sauvy in 1952) expressed solidarity among developing countries. However, it became fragmented by different political systems (democracies, military regimes, communist states), economic paths (oil-rich countries after 1973, newly industrialised countries, poor countries), regional conflicts and the end of the Cold War.

East Asia's rise: Japan's postwar recovery to become the second-largest economy; South Korea and Taiwan's export-led industrialisation; and later the rise of China showed that some developing countries could achieve rapid growth through state-guided capitalism, education and exports. This contrasted with the slower growth of many other Third World countries and changed the global economy.

sections.title: China, North Korea and Latin America

blocks.text:
The Sino-Soviet alliance weakened because of ideological and strategic conflict. Revolutionary China sought influence in the Third World, while North Korea maintained a highly centralised political system.

In Latin America, US policy interacted with local struggles over inequality, nationalism and socialism. Guatemala, Cuba, Chile and Nicaragua became major Cold War cases.

These examples show that the Cold War was not only a European conflict; it deeply shaped politics across the developing world.

Sino-Soviet split and China: ideological differences (de-Stalinisation, peaceful coexistence), Mao's rejection of the Soviet model, the withdrawal of Soviet advisers (1960), nuclear disputes and border clashes (1969) broke the alliance. China supported revolutionary movements in Asia and Africa (and built the TAZARA railway in Tanzania-Zambia), competed with the USSR for influence in the Third World and moved closer to the USA (1971-1972). North Korea under Kim Il-sung, Kim Jong-il and Kim Jong-un developed the Juche ideology, a hereditary dictatorship, a militarised economy and nuclear weapons.

Latin America: deep inequality, land concentration and foreign economic domination produced reformist and revolutionary movements. The USA, fearing communism, intervened: the CIA coup in Guatemala (1954), the Bay of Pigs and the embargo against Cuba, support for the Pinochet coup in Chile (1973) and funding of the Contras in Nicaragua (1980s). It also supported military dictatorships in Brazil (1964), Argentina (1976, the 'Dirty War') and elsewhere, through Operation Condor.

Significance: the Cold War was a global conflict fought largely in the developing world through proxy wars, coups and aid, with immense human costs. Local factors - nationalism, social inequality, ethnic and religious divisions - interacted with superpower rivalry. Studying these cases helps explain present-day politics in Asia, Africa and Latin America.
The Qing dynasty weakened under internal rebellion, foreign pressure and political and economic difficulties.

The Qing (Manchu) dynasty ruled China from 1644. In the nineteenth century, it faced population pressure, corruption, a weak treasury and rebellions. The First Opium War (1839-1842), caused by the British opium trade and Commissioner Lin Zexu's destruction of opium at Canton, ended with the Treaty of Nanking (1842), which ceded Hong Kong to Britain, opened five treaty ports, imposed indemnities and fixed tariffs - the first of the 'unequal treaties'. The Second Opium War (1856-1860) led to further concessions and the burning of the Summer Palace.

The Taiping Rebellion (1850-1864), led by Hong Xiuquan, who claimed to be the brother of Jesus, killed about 20-30 million people. Other rebellions included the Nian and Muslim revolts. The Self-Strengthening Movement (1861-1895) tried to adopt Western technology but was limited. Defeat by Japan (1894-1895) and the 'scramble for concessions' showed Qing weakness. The Hundred Days' Reform (1898) of Emperor Guangxu was crushed by Empress Dowager Cixi.
The Boxer uprising was an anti-foreign and anti-Christian movement that led to international military intervention.

The 'Boxers' (Society of Righteous and Harmonious Fists, Yihetuan) arose in Shandong in 1898-1899 among peasants suffering from drought, floods and economic hardship. They practised martial arts and believed they were immune to bullets, and blamed foreigners and Chinese Christians for China's troubles, with the slogan 'Support the Qing, destroy the foreign'.

In 1900, they killed missionaries, Chinese Christians and foreigners, and besieged the foreign legations in Beijing; Empress Dowager Cixi supported them and declared war on the foreign powers. An Eight-Nation Alliance (Britain, France, Germany, Russia, the USA, Japan, Italy and Austria-Hungary) sent about 20,000 troops, captured Beijing and lifted the siege (August 1900). The Boxer Protocol (1901) imposed a huge indemnity (450 million taels), allowed foreign troops in Beijing and ordered the execution of officials. The rebellion further weakened the Qing and led to the late Qing reforms (abolition of the civil service examinations in 1905).
The 1911 Revolution ended imperial rule and opened the republican period.

The late Qing reforms (constitutional plans, new army, education) came too late. Revolutionary groups, especially Sun Yat-sen's Tongmenghui (Revolutionary Alliance, 1905), spread anti-Manchu and republican ideas among students, overseas Chinese and soldiers. Anger over the nationalisation of railways (the Railway Protection Movement in Sichuan) and an accidental explosion at Wuchang led to an army mutiny on 10 October 1911 (the Wuchang Uprising, celebrated as 'Double Ten').

Provinces declared independence one after another. Sun Yat-sen returned from abroad and was elected Provisional President of the Republic of China at Nanjing (1 January 1912). To avoid civil war and secure the abdication, Sun agreed that Yuan Shikai, the powerful general of the Beiyang Army, would become president. The last emperor, Puyi (aged six), abdicated on 12 February 1912, ending over 2,000 years of imperial rule.
The Republic was established after the fall of the Qing but faced political fragmentation and instability.

Yuan Shikai became president (1912) but became increasingly authoritarian; he suppressed the Kuomintang (KMT, the Nationalist Party formed in 1912), whose leader Song Jiaoren was assassinated (1913), and declared himself emperor (1915-1916), but was forced to abandon the plan and died in 1916. China then fell into the 'warlord era' (1916-1928), when regional military leaders controlled different areas and the Beijing government was weak.

Japan's Twenty-One Demands (1915) and the Versailles Treaty's transfer of German rights in Shandong to Japan provoked the May Fourth Movement (4 May 1919), when students protested in Beijing. It became a broader New Culture Movement, criticising Confucianism and promoting science, democracy, vernacular literature (Lu Xun) and new ideas, including Marxism. This intellectual ferment led to the founding of the CCP (1921) and the reorganisation of the KMT.
Sun Yat-sen was a major revolutionary leader associated with the founding ideals of republican China.

Sun Yat-sen (1866-1925), born in Guangdong and educated in Hawaii and Hong Kong as a doctor, founded the Revive China Society (1894) and later the Tongmenghui (1905). He led several failed uprisings and raised funds among overseas Chinese. He became Provisional President in 1912 but gave the presidency to Yuan Shikai.

Later he established a government in Guangzhou (Canton), reorganised the KMT with Soviet help, formed the First United Front with the CCP (1923-1924) and founded the Whampoa Military Academy (1924), with Chiang Kai-shek as commandant and Zhou Enlai as head of the political department. He died in 1925 while trying to negotiate national unity. Both the KMT and the CCP honour him as the 'Father of the Nation' (Guofu) of modern China.
Sun's Three Principles are commonly expressed as nationalism, democracy and people's livelihood.

Sun Yat-sen's Three Principles of the People (Sanmin Zhuyi), developed from around 1905 and elaborated in lectures in 1924: (1) Minzu - nationalism: freeing China from Manchu rule and foreign imperialism, and achieving unity of China's ethnic groups; (2) Minquan - democracy or people's rights: a republic with elections and a constitution with five branches of government (executive, legislative, judicial, examination and control); and (3) Minsheng - people's livelihood: social welfare, equalisation of land rights (land value tax) and regulation of capital, sometimes described as a form of socialism.

He proposed three stages of revolution: military rule, political tutelage (under the party) and constitutional government. The principles became the official ideology of the KMT and remain influential in Taiwan's constitution.
The Northern Expedition was a Nationalist military campaign aimed at defeating warlords and unifying China.

In July 1926, the National Revolutionary Army of the KMT, led by Chiang Kai-shek and supported by the CCP and Soviet advisers (Mikhail Borodin), launched the Northern Expedition from Guangzhou to defeat the warlords and unify China. It quickly captured Wuhan, Nanjing and Shanghai, helped by peasant and worker uprisings organised by the communists.

In April 1927, Chiang turned against the communists in the Shanghai Massacre, killing thousands of communists and union workers, ending the First United Front. He established the Nationalist government at Nanjing. The expedition continued and captured Beijing (renamed Beiping) in 1928, and the Manchurian warlord Zhang Xueliang accepted Nationalist authority, formally unifying China under the KMT, although many warlords retained local power.
Chiang became the dominant Nationalist leader and headed the Kuomintang government through major periods of conflict.

Chiang Kai-shek (Jiang Jieshi, 1887-1975) studied military science in Japan, became commandant of the Whampoa Military Academy and, after Sun Yat-sen's death, leader of the KMT. He led the Northern Expedition, broke with the communists (1927), and established the Nanjing government (the 'Nanjing Decade', 1927-1937), which modernised some infrastructure but was authoritarian, corrupt and dependent on landlords and businessmen. He launched 'encirclement campaigns' against the communists and promoted the New Life Movement (1934), based on Confucian values.

In the Xi'an Incident (December 1936), he was kidnapped by Zhang Xueliang and forced to form a Second United Front with the communists against Japan. During the Sino-Japanese War (1937-1945), he moved the capital to Chongqing and received Allied support. After defeat in the Civil War (1949), he retreated to Taiwan, ruled as President of the Republic of China under martial law until his death in 1975, and was succeeded by his son Chiang Ching-kuo.
The CCP emerged in the early twentieth century and eventually became the principal revolutionary rival of the Nationalists.

The CCP was founded in Shanghai in July 1921 by Chen Duxiu, Li Dazhao and others, including Mao Zedong as a delegate, with help from the Comintern. It initially worked with the KMT (First United Front), organising workers and peasants. After the 1927 massacre, it built rural soviets, especially the Jiangxi Soviet (1931-1934), and the Red Army.

Under Mao's leadership (confirmed at the Zunyi Conference, 1935), the CCP developed a strategy of peasant-based revolution and guerrilla warfare rather than urban uprisings (a departure from orthodox Marxism). From its base at Yan'an, it carried out land reform, rectification campaigns and mass mobilisation. During the war against Japan, its membership grew from about 40,000 (1937) to over 1.2 million (1945). It won the Civil War (1946-1949) and has ruled the People's Republic since 1949.
Mao became the leading figure of the Chinese Communist Revolution and later the People's Republic of China.

Mao Zedong (1893-1976), son of a well-off peasant in Hunan, became a Marxist in Beijing, was a founding member of the CCP and organised peasants (his 'Report on the Peasant Movement in Hunan', 1927). He developed 'Mao Zedong Thought' - adapting Marxism-Leninism to Chinese conditions, with peasants as the main revolutionary force, protracted people's war ('political power grows out of the barrel of a gun'), the mass line and New Democracy.

As Chairman of the CCP and the PRC (from 1949), he led land reform, the campaigns against 'counter-revolutionaries', the first Five-Year Plan (1953-1957), the Hundred Flowers Campaign (1956-1957) and the Anti-Rightist Campaign, the Great Leap Forward (1958-1962) and the Cultural Revolution (1966-1976). His 'Little Red Book' (Quotations from Chairman Mao) became a symbol of the personality cult. He died on 9 September 1976. The CCP's 1981 resolution assessed him as '70 percent right, 30 percent wrong'.
The Long March was a major Communist retreat and regrouping that became central to CCP revolutionary memory.

In October 1934, facing Chiang's fifth encirclement campaign, about 86,000 members of the Red Army broke out of the Jiangxi Soviet. Over the next year they marched about 10,000 kilometres (12,500 km by some counts) through mountains, rivers and marshes across 11 provinces, fighting KMT and warlord forces, and crossing the Dadu River (Luding Bridge) and the Great Snowy Mountains. In January 1935, at the Zunyi Conference, Mao gained leadership of the party.

In October 1935, about 7,000-8,000 survivors reached Shaanxi in the north-west and established a base at Yan'an. Despite enormous losses, the march preserved the communist leadership, spread communist ideas among peasants along the route and became a heroic legend of endurance and commitment. Edgar Snow's 'Red Star Over China' (1937) spread the story internationally.
The People's Republic was established in 1949 after Communist victory in the civil war.

Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China on 1 October 1949. The new government, with Zhou Enlai as Premier, carried out land reform (1950-1953), redistributing land from landlords to peasants (with perhaps one to two million landlords killed), introduced the Marriage Law (1950) giving women equal rights and banning arranged marriages, launched campaigns against corruption and capitalists (Three-Anti and Five-Anti campaigns), and nationalised industry.

China signed the Sino-Soviet Treaty (1950), fought in the Korean War (1950-1953), took control of Tibet (1950-1951), and implemented the First Five-Year Plan (1953-1957) on the Soviet model, emphasising heavy industry. Agriculture was collectivised into cooperatives (1955-1956). The 1954 Constitution established the National People's Congress. Relations with India included Panchsheel (1954), but deteriorated with the Tibetan uprising (1959), the Dalai Lama's flight to India and the 1962 border war.
The Great Leap Forward attempted rapid economic transformation but produced severe disruption and suffering.

Launched in 1958, the Great Leap Forward aimed to rapidly overtake Britain in industrial production within fifteen years by mobilising China's huge labour force. About 700 million peasants were organised into some 26,000 people's communes, with communal kitchens. Backyard furnaces were set up to produce steel, but much of it was useless. Unrealistic targets, false reports of production, the diversion of labour from agriculture, Lysenkoist farming methods, the 'four pests' campaign (killing sparrows, which led to insect plagues) and continued grain exports caused disaster.

The resulting Great Chinese Famine (1959-1961) killed an estimated 15 to 45 million people, the deadliest famine in history. When Defence Minister Peng Dehuai criticised the policy at the Lushan Conference (1959), he was purged. Mao stepped back from day-to-day leadership; Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping introduced pragmatic recovery policies (allowing private plots and markets). The failure contributed to the Sino-Soviet split and later to Mao's attempt to regain power through the Cultural Revolution.
The Cultural Revolution was a radical political and social campaign that caused widespread upheaval.

The Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution (1966-1976) was launched by Mao to restore his authority, purge 'capitalist roaders' and 'revisionists' in the party (such as Liu Shaoqi, who died in prison, and Deng Xiaoping, who was sent to work in a factory), and renew revolutionary spirit. Students formed Red Guards, who attacked teachers, officials and intellectuals, and destroyed the 'Four Olds' (old customs, culture, habits and ideas) - temples, books and historical relics. Schools and universities closed; millions of urban youth were 'sent down' to the countryside.

The Gang of Four, led by Mao's wife Jiang Qing, controlled culture and propaganda. Factional violence led to near civil war, and the army was used to restore order (1967-1969). Lin Biao, Mao's designated successor, died in a plane crash in 1971 after an alleged coup attempt. Hundreds of thousands to perhaps two million people died. After Mao's death (1976), the Gang of Four was arrested. The CCP later called the Cultural Revolution a 'catastrophe' that caused 'the most severe setback and the heaviest losses' since 1949.
Deng led major economic reforms after the Mao era and moved China toward market-oriented policies while maintaining Communist Party rule.

Deng Xiaoping (1904-1997), a veteran of the Long March, was purged twice during the Cultural Revolution, but emerged as China's paramount leader by 1978 (Third Plenum of the Eleventh Central Committee). He promoted the 'Four Modernisations' (agriculture, industry, defence, science and technology) and pragmatic policies ('It does not matter whether a cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice').

Reforms: the household responsibility system replaced collective farming; township and village enterprises grew; Special Economic Zones (Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Shantou, Xiamen, 1980) opened to foreign investment; prices were gradually freed; and China joined the world economy. The 'one-child policy' (1979) controlled population growth. Deng called this 'socialism with Chinese characteristics'. Economic growth averaged about 10 percent a year, lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty. Politically, he rejected democracy, insisting on the 'Four Cardinal Principles' (socialism, dictatorship of the proletariat, party leadership, Marxism-Leninism-Mao Zedong Thought). His 'Southern Tour' (1992) revived reforms. He negotiated the return of Hong Kong (1997) under 'one country, two systems'.
The 1989 protests demanded political and social reforms and were suppressed by the state.

In April 1989, after the death of the reformist leader Hu Yaobang, students gathered in Tiananmen Square in Beijing to mourn him and demand political reform, freedom of the press, an end to corruption and dialogue with the government. Workers and citizens joined; protests spread to many cities. Students began a hunger strike in May, during Soviet leader Gorbachev's visit, and erected a 'Goddess of Democracy' statue. General Secretary Zhao Ziyang sympathised with the students but was removed.

The government declared martial law (20 May). On the night of 3-4 June 1989, the People's Liberation Army moved into central Beijing with tanks and troops and fired on protesters; estimates of the dead range from several hundred to several thousand. The image of 'Tank Man' became famous worldwide. Leaders were arrested or fled abroad. Western countries imposed sanctions. The government later strengthened party control, promoted patriotic education and accelerated economic reforms, while the event remains heavily censored in China.
Rapid economic growth and expanding international influence made China a major global power.

After Deng, Jiang Zemin (1989-2002) and Hu Jintao (2002-2012) continued economic reform. China joined the World Trade Organization (2001), became the 'workshop of the world' and the largest exporter, and in 2010 overtook Japan to become the world's second-largest economy. It hosted the 2008 Beijing Olympics and the 2010 Shanghai Expo, launched human spaceflight (2003) and expanded investment abroad.

Under Xi Jinping (General Secretary from 2012, President from 2013), China launched the Belt and Road Initiative (2013), a massive infrastructure and investment programme across Asia, Africa and Europe, founded the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (2016), modernised its military, became more assertive in the South China Sea and on its borders (including the clash with India at Galwan in 2020), and increased its role in international organisations. China is now a major global power competing with the USA in trade, technology and strategic influence.
Contemporary China combines major economic strength and international influence with internal social, political and developmental challenges.

Achievements: China became the world's largest manufacturer and trading nation, eliminated extreme poverty according to its official standards (2020), built the world's largest high-speed rail network, and became a leader in technologies such as renewable energy, electric vehicles and telecommunications (5G). Under Xi Jinping, the party strengthened its control, removed presidential term limits (2018), promoted 'Xi Jinping Thought' and launched an anti-corruption campaign.

Challenges: income inequality and rural-urban gaps; an ageing population and shrinking workforce (the one-child policy was replaced by a two-child policy in 2016 and a three-child policy in 2021); environmental pollution; a property sector crisis (Evergrande); slowing growth; tensions with the USA (trade war from 2018, technology restrictions) and neighbours; international criticism over human rights in Xinjiang (treatment of Uyghurs), Tibet and Hong Kong (the National Security Law of 2020); and the question of Taiwan.
