China's future role in the world remains a central issue in global politics.

sections.title: End of Imperial China and the Republic

blocks.text:
Modern China entered a period of crisis as the Qing dynasty faced foreign pressure and internal weakness. The Boxer Rebellion revealed strong anti-foreign tensions but ended with international intervention.

The 1911 Revolution brought the Qing dynasty to an end and established the Republic of China. Sun Yat-sen's Three Principles of the People became important republican ideals.

Political fragmentation continued, and the Northern Expedition later strengthened Chiang Kai-shek and the Nationalists.

Decline of the Qing: internal problems (population pressure, corruption, rebellions - especially the Taiping Rebellion) combined with foreign aggression (Opium Wars and unequal treaties, the loss to Japan in 1894-1895, the scramble for concessions). The Self-Strengthening Movement and the Hundred Days' Reform (1898) failed due to conservative resistance led by Empress Dowager Cixi. The Boxer Rebellion (1899-1901), an anti-foreign peasant movement, was crushed by the Eight-Nation Alliance and led to the humiliating Boxer Protocol.

1911 Revolution: late Qing reforms (abolition of the examination system in 1905, plans for a constitution) came too late; Sun Yat-sen's Tongmenghui spread republican ideas; the Wuchang Uprising (10 October 1911) led to the collapse of the dynasty and the establishment of the Republic (1912), with Sun as Provisional President, followed by Yuan Shikai. Sun's Three Principles - nationalism, democracy and people's livelihood - became the ideology of the KMT.

Republic and warlords: Yuan's dictatorship and failed imperial attempt, the warlord era (1916-1928), Japan's Twenty-One Demands, and the May Fourth Movement (1919) with its New Culture ideas. Sun reorganised the KMT with Soviet help and formed the First United Front with the CCP. After his death, Chiang Kai-shek led the Northern Expedition (1926-1928), broke with the communists (1927) and established the Nationalist government at Nanjing, nominally unifying China.

The Chinese Communist Party emerged as a major revolutionary movement. Mao Zedong became its leading figure, while the Long March helped preserve and reshape Communist leadership.

Long conflict between Communists and Nationalists eventually ended in Communist victory on the mainland. In 1949, the People's Republic of China was established.

The revolution fundamentally changed China's political and social system.

Origins: the CCP was founded in 1921, influenced by the May Fourth Movement and the Russian Revolution. After Chiang's 1927 purge, it shifted to rural bases. Mao developed a peasant-based strategy and guerrilla warfare in the Jiangxi Soviet. The Long March (1934-1935) preserved the party and established Mao's leadership (Zunyi, 1935); Yan'an became the communist base, where the party developed its ideology, organisation and popular support.

War and civil war: the Japanese invasion of Manchuria (1931) and full-scale war (1937) created nationalist sentiment. The Xi'an Incident (1936) led to the Second United Front. The communists gained support through guerrilla resistance against Japan, land reform (rent reduction), disciplined troops and mass mobilisation, while the KMT suffered from corruption, inflation, defeats and dependence on landlords. In the Civil War (1946-1949), decisive battles (Liaoshen, Huaihai, Pingjin) gave the communists victory.

1949 and its significance: Mao proclaimed the PRC on 1 October 1949; the KMT retreated to Taiwan. The revolution ended a century of foreign humiliation, unified the country, and transformed China's society through land reform, collectivisation, nationalisation and women's legal rights. It also brought one-party rule and political campaigns that caused great suffering.

sections.title: Mao Era: Great Leap Forward and Cultural Revolution

blocks.text:
The Great Leap Forward attempted rapid industrial and agricultural transformation. Its failures caused major economic disruption and human suffering.

The Cultural Revolution later mobilised radical political campaigns against alleged enemies and old institutions, producing deep social and educational upheaval.

Both movements were strongly connected with Mao's leadership and remain central to understanding the costs and contradictions of revolutionary China.

Great Leap Forward (1958-1962): Mao's attempt to industrialise rapidly through mass mobilisation, people's communes and backyard steel furnaces, rejecting the Soviet model. Unrealistic targets, exaggerated reports, disruption of agriculture and continued grain procurement caused the Great Famine (1959-1961), in which tens of millions died. Peng Dehuai's criticism led to his purge. Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping's recovery policies followed, reducing Mao's influence temporarily.

Cultural Revolution (1966-1976): Mao mobilised Red Guards against party leaders, intellectuals and 'old' culture, purged Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping, closed schools and universities, and sent millions of youth to the countryside. The Gang of Four dominated; factional violence spread; the army restored order; Lin Biao died (1971). Cultural heritage was destroyed, education and the economy suffered, and millions were persecuted. It ended with Mao's death and the arrest of the Gang of Four (1976).

Evaluation: both movements were driven by Mao's utopian vision of rapid transformation and permanent revolution, and his struggle with party rivals. They caused enormous human suffering and economic damage. The CCP's 1981 resolution blamed Mao for the Cultural Revolution while upholding his overall historical role. These experiences shaped Deng's later emphasis on pragmatism, stability and economic development.

sections.title: Deng Xiaoping and China in the 21st Century

blocks.text:
Deng Xiaoping introduced economic reforms that expanded market mechanisms and opened China more widely to international trade and investment. Economic growth accelerated dramatically.

The Tiananmen Square protests of 1989 showed continuing tensions surrounding political reform. In the twenty-first century, China has become a major global economic and political power.

Its rise also brings challenges involving inequality, development, governance and its changing role in world affairs.

Deng's reforms (from 1978): the Four Modernisations; decollectivisation and the household responsibility system; township and village enterprises; Special Economic Zones (Shenzhen, 1980) and opening to foreign investment; gradual price reform; and 'socialism with Chinese characteristics'. China achieved extraordinary growth, lifting hundreds of millions from poverty. Politically, the party maintained its monopoly of power.

Tiananmen (1989): students and workers demanded political reform and an end to corruption; the government imposed martial law and the army crushed the protests (3-4 June). After this, the party combined continued economic liberalisation (Deng's Southern Tour, 1992) with strict political control and patriotic education. Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) returned to China under 'one country, two systems'.

China in the twenty-first century: WTO membership (2001), becoming the second-largest economy (2010), the Belt and Road Initiative, technological advances and military modernisation have made China a global power. Under Xi Jinping, central control has increased, term limits were removed, and China has become more assertive internationally. Challenges include inequality, an ageing population, environmental problems, slowing growth, human rights criticism (Xinjiang, Hong Kong, Tibet), the Taiwan question and rivalry with the USA and neighbours, including India.
The field studies the region's past through material remains while taking account of its distinctive geography, cultural diversity and links with South and Southeast Asia.

Northeast India is a meeting point of South Asia, East Asia and Southeast Asia, so its archaeology is important for understanding the movement of people, crops (such as rice), technologies (shouldered celts, cord-marked pottery) and cultural practices (megaliths). Its archaeology is still less developed than other parts of India because of thick forests, heavy rainfall that destroys organic remains, steep terrain, acidic soils, political instability, and limited institutional support.

Key themes include the prehistoric stone-tool traditions, the Neolithic and its links with Southeast Asia, living megalithic traditions among the Khasis, Nagas and others, and the historical archaeology of Kamarupa, the Ahoms, Koches, Chutiyas, Kacharis, Manipur and Tripura. Mizoram has sites such as Vangchhia in Champhai district, with standing stones and carvings, which have been studied by the Archaeological Survey of India.

sections.title: History of Archaeology in the Northeast

blocks.text: Archaeological research in the region developed gradually through surveys, excavations and specialised studies of prehistoric and historical remains.

Colonial period: early reports by British officers, such as John Lubbock's note on stone tools from the Naga Hills (1867), J. H. Hutton's and J. P. Mills's ethnographic studies, which documented megaliths of the Khasis and Nagas, and P. R. T. Gurdon's work on the Khasis (1907). The Archaeological Survey surveyed historical monuments in Assam (such as at Tezpur and Sivasagar), and Kanaklal Barua and others studied Assamese history.

Postcolonial period: systematic excavations began, for example at Daojali Hading in the North Cachar Hills (Dima Hasao district of Assam, by M. C. Goswami and T. C. Sharma, 1961-1963), Sarutaru near Guwahati, and Ambari in Guwahati. Gauhati University's Department of Anthropology, the North-Eastern Hill University (NEHU) in Shillong and state archaeology departments developed research. Scholars such as T. C. Sharma, Dilip K. Medhi, Manjil Hazarika ('Prehistory and Archaeology of Northeast India', 2017), Tiatoshi Jamir and Pamela Jamir in Nagaland and others have developed the field.
Archaeologists use different theoretical approaches to interpret material culture, settlement, technology and human behaviour.

Culture-historical approaches classified tools and pottery to define cultures and timelines, often assuming that cultural traits spread by diffusion or migration, for example explaining the Northeast Neolithic as derived from Southeast Asia. Processual approaches emphasised environmental adaptation, subsistence and systems (for example, studying how jhum cultivation and settlement patterns related to ecology).

Post-processual and interpretive approaches focus on meanings, symbols and social identities - useful for studying megaliths as markers of memory, status and community. Ethnoarchaeology is particularly important in the Northeast because many communities still practise traditions such as megalith-building, pottery-making, jhum cultivation and weaving, which help interpret archaeological evidence. Postcolonial and indigenous approaches question colonial assumptions and involve communities.
Evidence from early stone-tool traditions forms part of the study of prehistoric Northeast India.

Palaeolithic tools have been found in the Garo Hills of Meghalaya (the Rongram valley, Ganol and Simsang river valleys), Tripura (Haora and Khowai valleys, where fossil-wood tools were used), Arunachal Pradesh (Kamla valley, Daphabum), Assam and Nagaland. Tools include choppers, handaxes and cleavers, often made of quartzite, dolerite and fossil wood. Their dating is uncertain because of a lack of absolute dates, though they may resemble the Hoabinhian and other Southeast Asian traditions.

Mesolithic and microlithic tools are reported from the Garo Hills (Selbalgiri), Tripura and other places. Some sites in the Garo Hills show a sequence from Palaeolithic to Neolithic. Northeast prehistory is connected both with the Soanian and Acheulian traditions of the subcontinent and with the pebble-tool traditions of Southeast Asia, but more research and dating are needed.
Neolithic archaeology includes developments in the Khasi, Jaintia and Garo Hills and wider questions of food production, settlement and technology.

The Northeast Neolithic is characterised by polished stone tools - especially shouldered celts (axes with shoulders for hafting) and rounded-butt axes - cord-marked and impressed pottery, grinding stones and evidence of cultivation, possibly of rice and other crops. Important sites include Daojali Hading (Dima Hasao, Assam), Sarutaru (Kamrup), Selbalgiri and other sites in the Garo Hills, sites in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills such as Pynthorlangtein, Napchik (Manipur), and sites in Nagaland and Arunachal (Parsi-Parlo).

Its features are similar to Southeast Asian and southern Chinese Neolithic traditions, suggesting connections through migration or exchange, possibly with Austroasiatic-speaking peoples (such as the ancestors of the Khasis). Dates are still debated: some estimates place the Northeast Neolithic between about 3000 and 1000 BCE, later than the Neolithic in western South Asia, and in some areas Neolithic-type tools continued until recent times. The Neolithic is linked with the origins of shifting cultivation and settled villages in the region.
Megaliths are important cultural remains in parts of Northeast India and are studied in relation to regional traditions and connections with South and Southeast Asia.

Megaliths ('big stones') include menhirs (standing stones), dolmens (table stones) and stone circles, erected for burial, commemoration of the dead, feasts of merit and village boundaries. The Northeast is remarkable for living megalithic traditions continuing into modern times. In Meghalaya, the Khasi and Jaintia people erected menhirs (mawbynna) and table stones (mawkynthei) for ancestors; the Nartiang monoliths in the Jaintia Hills include some of the tallest in the region. The Nagas erected stones to commemorate feasts of merit and the dead (such as at Willong Khullen in Manipur). The Dimasa Kacharis' carved stone pillars stand at Kasomari (Dimapur).

In Mizoram, the Vangchhia site in Champhai district has many menhirs, some with carvings of humans, animals and weapons, associated with commemoration and possibly the Thangchhuah feasts; other memorial stones (lungdawh) are found across Mizoram. Scholars compare these traditions with megaliths in Indonesia (Sumba, Nias), Laos (Plain of Jars) and South India, raising questions about connections between South and Southeast Asia.
Archaeology examines how communities obtained food and how tools and technologies changed through time.

Prehistoric people in the Northeast lived by hunting, gathering and fishing in forests and rivers, using stone tools and probably bamboo and wood (which rarely survive). Neolithic communities began cultivating crops - perhaps rice, millet, taro and yams - and domesticating animals like pigs and chickens. Shifting cultivation (jhum), still practised today, probably has prehistoric roots.

Technologies include stone tools (from flaked choppers to polished shouldered celts), pottery (handmade cord-marked wares and later wheel-made wares), bamboo and cane crafts, weaving, iron-working (the Khasi Hills had an important traditional iron-smelting industry, studied at sites near Nongkrem and Mawmluh, possibly dating back over a thousand years) and salt production (salt springs in Nagaland and Manipur). Ethnoarchaeology of present communities helps understand these ancient technologies.
Material remains of the Ahom kingdom help reconstruct political, architectural and cultural history in the Brahmaputra Valley.

The Ahoms (1228-1826) left important material remains: the maidams (mound burials) of Ahom kings and nobles at Charaideo (Sivasagar district), sometimes called the 'pyramids of Assam', which were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2024 - the first cultural site of the Northeast on the list. In Sivasagar (Rangpur) and Gargaon: the Rang Ghar (an amphitheatre for royal games, built under Pramatta Singha, often called Asia's oldest surviving amphitheatre), the Talatal Ghar (a multi-storeyed palace with underground floors, built under Rudra Singha and Rajeswar Singha) and the Kareng Ghar at Gargaon.

Temples include the Sivadol, Vishnudol and Devidol at Sivasagar (built by Queen Ambika in the 1730s) and many others. The Ahoms built large tanks (Sivasagar, Joysagar, Gourisagar), roads (Ali) and embankments, and used burnt bricks with a lime-based mortar (with ingredients such as eggs and black gram, according to tradition). Coins, weapons (cannons), manuscripts (buranjis) and copper plate inscriptions add to the evidence.
Architecture and material culture provide evidence for the ancient kingdom of Kamarupa.

Kamarupa (also called Pragjyotisha) was an ancient kingdom in the Brahmaputra valley, mentioned in Samudragupta's Allahabad Pillar inscription (fourth century) as a frontier state. It was ruled by the Varman dynasty (c. 350-650, including Bhaskaravarman), the Mlechchha (Salastambha) dynasty (c. 650-900) and the Pala dynasty (c. 900-1100). Capitals included Pragjyotishpur (Guwahati), Haruppeshwara (Tezpur) and Durjaya.

Archaeological remains: the Da Parbatia door frame near Tezpur (c. fifth-sixth century), carved in the Gupta style with figures of Ganga and Yamuna, is one of the earliest sculptural remains; the ruins of Madan Kamdev (Kamrup), with erotic and religious sculptures (tenth-twelfth centuries); excavations at Ambari in Guwahati, which revealed sculptures, pottery and structures from the seventh to twelfth centuries; Surya Pahar (Goalpara), with rock-cut Hindu, Buddhist and Jain images; and Bamuni Hills at Tezpur. The Kamakhya temple in Guwahati, rebuilt in later centuries, stands on an ancient site.
The material contributions of the Koch and Chutiya dynasties form part of the archaeology of historical Northeast India.

The Koch dynasty, founded by Bishwa Singha (c. 1515) in western Assam and north Bengal (Cooch Behar), reached its height under Naranarayana (1540-1586) and his brother and general Chilarai, who conquered large areas. Naranarayana rebuilt the Kamakhya temple (1565) after its destruction, and the Koches patronised Srimanta Sankardeva and Vaishnavism. They issued silver coins (Narayani tanka) and built the Hayagriva Madhava temple at Hajo. The kingdom later split into Koch Bihar and Koch Hajo.

The Chutiya kingdom ruled eastern Assam and parts of Arunachal (Sadiya) from about the twelfth or thirteenth century until it was conquered by the Ahoms in 1523-1524. Remains associated with them include the Tamreswari temple (the 'copper temple') near Sadiya, Bhismaknagar fort near Roing (Arunachal Pradesh), with brick structures, and the Malinithan temple site at Likabali (Arunachal), with sculptures from around the thirteenth-fourteenth centuries. Students should note that some attributions are debated.
Prehistoric rock art provides evidence of symbolic and artistic activity and must be studied within its archaeological context.

Rock art includes paintings (pictographs) and engravings (petroglyphs) on rock surfaces. In the Northeast, rock art is less studied than in central India (Bhimbetka), but examples have been reported in Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Assam, Manipur and Mizoram; they include engravings of human figures, animals, weapons and geometric designs. The rock-cut relief sculptures of Unakoti in Tripura (seventh-ninth centuries or later), including huge carved faces of Shiva and other deities, are a major site of rock-cut art, though religious and historical rather than prehistoric.

Dating and interpretation of rock art are difficult; archaeologists study its style, context, weathering and local traditions. In Mizoram, carvings on stones at sites such as Vangchhia show human figures and animals, linked with memorial traditions. Rock art provides evidence of symbolic thought, belief and social life.
Epigraphical evidence from Ahom, Kamarupa and Koch contexts contributes to historical reconstruction.

Kamarupa inscriptions include the Umachal rock inscription of Surendravarman (fifth century, in Guwahati), the earliest inscription found in Assam; the Nagajari-Khanikargaon inscription; the Doobi and Nidhanpur copper plates of Bhaskaravarman, which give the genealogy of the Varman kings; the Tezpur rock inscription of Harjaravarman (829 CE) and copper plates of the Pala kings. Most are in Sanskrit, using the Gupta-derived script, and record land grants and royal genealogies.

Ahom inscriptions include copper plates, stone inscriptions in temples and coins with legends in Ahom script, Sanskrit and Assamese, together with the buranjis (chronicles). Koch inscriptions include the Kamakhya temple inscription of Naranarayana (1565) and coins. Epigraphy helps reconstruct dynasties, land grants, religion, administration and the spread of Sanskrit culture in the region.
Buddhist cave art forms part of the region's material evidence for religious and artistic traditions.

Buddhist remains in the Northeast include the Pilak site in southern Tripura (eighth-twelfth centuries), with terracotta plaques and Buddhist and Hindu sculptures, showing links with the Buddhist art of Bengal and Myanmar; Boxanagar (Tripura) with Buddhist stupa remains; and Surya Pahar in Goalpara (Assam), with rock-cut images and votive stupas. In Arunachal Pradesh and Sikkim, Tibetan Buddhist monasteries such as Tawang (founded in 1680-1681) and Rumtek have murals, thangka paintings and sculptures.

Hiuen Tsang's account mentions that Buddhism was less prominent in Kamarupa, though the king respected Buddhist scholars. Buddhist art of the region shows connections with Pala art of Bengal, Tibetan traditions and Southeast Asian (Burmese) styles. Students should refer to the prescribed readings for specific cave art sites included in the syllabus.
Postcolonial approaches question older colonial interpretations and seek to understand archaeology through regional histories and power relations.

Postcolonial archaeology critiques the colonial legacy in research: colonial scholars often viewed Northeast communities as 'primitive' and 'unchanging', interpreted their past through diffusion from outside, and focused on monuments associated with Sanskritic or Ahom states while ignoring hill communities. Colonial collecting also removed artefacts to museums abroad.

Postcolonial approaches aim to write regional histories from local perspectives, recognise the agency and complexity of hill and valley societies, question the categories of 'tribe' and 'civilisation', examine how archaeology has been used in nation-building and identity politics, and address the repatriation of objects (such as Naga human remains held in Oxford's Pitt Rivers Museum, which began to be discussed with Naga communities in the 2020s).
Indigenous approaches give greater importance to local knowledge, community perspectives and cultural ownership.

Indigenous archaeology involves indigenous communities in the research process and respects their knowledge, values and rights. It recognises oral traditions, genealogies, place names and traditional knowledge as valuable sources of history, and seeks to make archaeology serve community interests, such as cultural revival and identity. It also respects sacred sites and objects.

In the Northeast, where many communities have strong oral traditions and living practices (such as megalith-building and jhum), indigenous archaeology is especially relevant. Examples include research in Nagaland by Naga archaeologists (Tiatoshi Jamir) working with village communities, and the documentation of village histories and migration sites. This approach can reduce suspicion of outsiders and produce more accurate interpretations.
Archaeological heritage can become connected with public policy, land claims, identity and community rights.

In the Northeast, land is often owned by communities, clans or chiefs under customary law, and protected by the Sixth Schedule, Article 371A (Nagaland), 371G (Mizoram) and others. Archaeological sites and evidence of past settlement can be used to support claims of ancestral territory, indigenous status or historical rights in boundary disputes between states and communities.

At the same time, designating sites as protected monuments under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act (1958) can restrict local land use, creating conflicts. Development projects (dams, roads, mining) may destroy sites, requiring heritage impact assessments. Archaeologists must therefore consider how their work affects public policy, land rights and community interests, and avoid their findings being misused in ethnic conflicts.
Research involving human remains requires ethical treatment, respect for communities and responsible scientific practice.

Human remains are especially sensitive. Many Northeast communities have specific beliefs about the dead, ancestors and burial sites. During the colonial period, human skulls and remains (including Naga trophy skulls) were collected and taken to museums in Britain and elsewhere without consent. Today, ethical guidelines require informed consent from communities, respect for remains, careful handling, limited destructive analysis and the possibility of reburial or repatriation.

Scientific analysis of remains, including DNA and isotopes, can provide valuable information about ancestry, migration, diet and health, but must be conducted responsibly and shared with the communities. International principles include the Vermillion Accord on Human Remains (World Archaeological Congress, 1989) and UNESCO guidelines. In India, there is a need for clearer laws and protocols.
Collaboration between archaeologists and local communities can improve research, interpretation and heritage conservation.

Collaborative or community archaeology involves local people at every stage - planning, excavation, interpretation, conservation and presentation. Benefits include access to local knowledge (oral history, traditional names, uses of land), better protection of sites by communities, greater trust, skill development and employment, and interpretations that reflect local perspectives. Community museums and heritage festivals can present the results.

Examples in the Northeast include village-based heritage projects in Nagaland and Meghalaya, collaboration between universities and village councils, and the involvement of local youth in surveys. Collaboration also requires respecting community decisions about sensitive sites and sharing benefits such as tourism income.
The syllabus emphasises the relevance of Northeast archaeology to local and global concerns and the need for future research and conservation.

Future directions include: more systematic surveys and excavations, especially in less explored areas such as Mizoram, Arunachal and Tripura; scientific dating (radiocarbon, luminescence) to build reliable chronologies; archaeobotany to study early agriculture, including the origins of rice cultivation; ancient DNA studies to understand population history and links with Southeast and East Asia; and remote sensing to locate sites under forest cover.

Other needs include protecting sites threatened by development, climate change and looting; developing museums and heritage tourism; training local archaeologists; integrating archaeology with oral traditions and ethnography; and connecting Northeast archaeology to global debates about migration, agriculture, megalithic traditions and state formation. The region's position between South, East and Southeast Asia makes its archaeology of global importance.

sections.title: Introduction and Prehistory of Northeast India

blocks.text:
The archaeology of Northeast India is shaped by the region's geography and cultural diversity. Its history of research includes changing archaeological methods and theoretical approaches.

Prehistoric study covers Palaeolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic cultures. The Khasi, Jaintia and Garo Hills are specifically included in the syllabus. Megalithic cultures are important for examining possible regional links with South and Southeast Asia.

Changes in subsistence and technology help reconstruct how prehistoric communities adapted to their environments.

Introduction: the Northeast's geography (hills, forests, high rainfall, rivers), cultural diversity and position between South and Southeast Asia shape its archaeology. Research began with colonial reports and ethnography (Lubbock, Hutton, Mills, Gurdon), followed by postcolonial excavations (Daojali Hading, Sarutaru, Ambari) and university research (Gauhati University, NEHU). Theoretical approaches include culture history, processual archaeology, interpretive and ethnoarchaeological approaches, and postcolonial and indigenous perspectives.

Prehistory: Palaeolithic tools from the Garo Hills (Rongram valley), Tripura (fossil wood tools), Arunachal and Assam; Mesolithic microliths in the Garo Hills; and a Neolithic with shouldered celts, polished axes and cord-marked pottery (Daojali Hading, Sarutaru, Selbalgiri, Khasi and Jaintia sites, Napchik in Manipur), with strong links to Southeast Asia and southern China. Dating remains a major problem.

Megalithic cultures: living traditions among the Khasis, Jaintias (Nartiang), Nagas, Dimasas (Kasomari pillars) and Mizos (Vangchhia), erected for the dead, feasts of merit and commemoration, comparable with Southeast Asian megaliths. Subsistence and technology: hunting-gathering, shifting cultivation, early rice and tuber cultivation, pottery, iron-smelting in the Khasi Hills and salt production. These show adaptation to a forested, hilly environment.

Historical archaeology includes the Ahom kingdom, Kamarupa and the Koch and Chutiya dynasties. Architecture, artefacts and other material remains provide evidence beyond written sources.

The syllabus also includes rock art, inscriptions and Buddhist cave art. Epigraphical studies help reconstruct political and cultural history, while art and architecture reveal religious and social traditions.

Together these materials broaden our understanding of Northeast India's historical past.

Kamarupa: an early historical kingdom (fourth-twelfth centuries) under the Varman, Salastambha and Pala dynasties; remains include the Da Parbatia door frame, Madan Kamdev, Ambari, Surya Pahar and Bamuni Hills; inscriptions include the Umachal rock inscription, the Nidhanpur and Doobi copper plates and the Tezpur inscription. These show the spread of Sanskritic religion and kingship in the region.

Ahoms (1228-1826): the maidams of Charaideo (UNESCO World Heritage, 2024), the Rang Ghar, Talatal Ghar and Kareng Ghar, the Sivadol temples, tanks, roads and embankments, coins and buranjis. Koches: Naranarayana's rebuilding of Kamakhya (1565), the Hajo temples and Narayani coins. Chutiyas: the Tamreswari temple, Bhismaknagar fort and Malinithan. Other kingdoms include the Kacharis (Dimapur and Maibang ruins), the Jaintia kingdom and Tripura (Udaipur temples).

Art and inscriptions: rock art and engravings (including Vangchhia carvings in Mizoram), rock-cut reliefs at Unakoti (Tripura), Buddhist remains at Pilak (Tripura) and Surya Pahar, and Tibetan Buddhist monastery art (Tawang). Epigraphy from Kamarupa, Ahom and Koch contexts helps reconstruct political and cultural history. Together, these materials show that Northeast India had complex states, religious traditions and artistic achievements, connected with both Bengal and Southeast Asia.

sections.title: Contemporary Perspectives on Northeast Indian Archaeology

blocks.text:
Contemporary archaeology increasingly uses postcolonial and Indigenous approaches. These approaches question older assumptions and give greater attention to local histories and community knowledge.

Archaeology can affect public policy, land rights and cultural heritage. Ethical questions are especially important in research involving human remains and culturally sensitive materials.

Collaborative work with local communities can strengthen both research and conservation. The future of Northeast archaeology therefore depends on responsible, locally engaged and scientifically careful practice.

Postcolonial and indigenous approaches: they question colonial views of Northeast communities as primitive and isolated, criticise the neglect of hill societies, address the repatriation of objects and human remains taken in colonial times, and give importance to oral traditions and local knowledge. They emphasise community participation and respect for sacred sites.

Public policy, land rights and ethics: archaeological evidence can be used in claims for ancestral land and identity and in boundary disputes, while heritage protection can restrict local land use. Development projects threaten sites. Ethical issues include treatment of human remains (consent, reburial, repatriation), responsible scientific analysis, and avoiding misuse of archaeology in ethnic politics.

Collaboration and future: collaborative research with village councils and communities improves interpretation and conservation; the future requires more surveys, scientific dating, archaeobotany, ancient DNA, remote sensing, local training, museums and heritage management. Responsible, locally engaged and scientifically careful archaeology can reveal the Northeast's significant role in Asian history, including the spread of agriculture, megalithic traditions and state formation.
